Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 47, verse 1:

[Surat Muhammad]
Thirty-nine verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah — He will render their deeds void.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah — He will render their deeds void.﴾

The beginning of this surah is connected to the end of the preceding surah, for its last verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. If someone says: how can the defiantly disobedient be destroyed when he has good deeds, such as feeding food, maintaining ties of kinship, and other things that a person does not free himself from throughout his life, so that destroying him would entail nullifying his deed? Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7], and He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah — He will render their deeds void﴾, meaning that nothing of their deed remains and nothing of it is found, so how is destruction not precluded? We will explain how the nullification of deeds occurs, along with a verification of the matter, and Allah is exalted above injustice. In the interpretation there are several issues:

The first issue: Who is meant by His saying ﴿those who disbelieve﴾? We say: there are several views. The first: they are those among them who used to feed the army on the day of Badr, among them Abu Jahl, al-Harith, the two sons of Hisham, Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and others. The second: the disbelievers of Quraysh. The third: the People of the Book. The fourth: it is general and includes every disbeliever.

The second issue: regarding "barring" (al-sadd) there are two aspects:

One of them: they barred themselves, meaning that they barred themselves from the path and prevented their intellects from following the proof.

The second: they barred others and prevented them, as He, exalted is He, said of the oppressed: ﴿Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers"﴾ [Saba': 31]. On this there is a question: nullification of deeds is connected to disbelief and barring, and the oppressed did not bar, so it would not nullify their deeds. We say: specification by mention does not indicate the negation of what is other than it, especially when what is mentioned is more deserving of mention than others, and here the disbelieving barrer is the one who was brought into corruption, so he is more deserving of mention. Or we say: every one who disbelieves becomes a barrer of others. As for the arrogant, this is evident; as for the oppressed, it is because by following him he established for the arrogant what prevents him from following the Messenger, for after he is followed, he becomes a follower. Also, every one who disbelieves becomes a barrer of those after him, because the custom of the disbelievers is to follow the previous ones, as He said of them: ﴿Rather, they said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22], or "emulating." If it is said: according to this, every disbeliever is a barrer, so what is the benefit of mentioning barring after disbelief? We say: it is of the type of mentioning the cause and conjoining the effect to it; you say: "I ate a lot and became full," and disbelief according to this is the cause of barring. Then, when we say that what is meant by it is that they barred themselves, there is an indication that what is within the souls of natural disposition (fitrah) was calling to faith, and refusal occurred due to an impediment, which is barring oneself.

The third issue: regarding that from which they were barred, there are several aspects:

The first: from spending on Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his companions.

The second: from jihad.

The third: from faith.

The fourth: from everything in which there is obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and that is following Muhammad, peace be upon him, because the Prophet ﷺ is one who guides to the straight path, and it is the path of Allah. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 52-53]. So whoever prevents others from following Muhammad, peace be upon him, has barred from the way of Allah.

The fourth issue: regarding "misguiding" (idlal) there are several aspects:

The first: what is meant by it is nullification (ibtal). Its basis is that the meaning is that He caused it to go astray such that he does not find it, for the seeker only seeks it in existence, and what is not found in existence is nonexistent. If it is said: how can Allah nullify a good deed that He Himself brought into being? We say: nullification has several aspects. One of them: He weighs their evil deeds against the good deeds that proceeded from them, and cancels them by the weighing, leaving them with pure evil deeds, because disbelief outweighs, among good deeds, what is other than faith, and faith outweighs, among evil deeds, what is other than disbelief.

The second: He nullified it because the condition of its establishment and affirmation was lacking, which is faith, for it is the condition of the acceptance of the deed. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. When Allah does not accept the deed, it has no existence, because the deed has no permanence in itself; rather it is annihilated immediately after it comes into being in reality. However, Allah, exalted is He, records with Himself, by His grace, that so-and-so did a righteous deed and that its reward is with Me, so it remains as a ruling. This remaining as a ruling is better than the remaining that belongs to bodies, which are the locus of deeds in reality, for although bodies remain, their end is to perish, whereas the righteous deed is among the enduring things with Allah forever. Once this is established, it becomes clear that Allah is bountiful in acceptance, and He has declared: "I accept only from a believer." Whoever acts and toils without prior faith, it is he who wastes his toil, not Allah, exalted is He.

The third: the disbeliever did not perform his deed for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, so he has brought no good. Thus His saying ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7] is not an objection against us. Its explanation is that a deed is distinguished only by reference to the one for whom the deed is done, not by the doer nor by the act itself. For whoever stands up to kill a person and it does not happen that he kills him, then stands up to honor him and the honoring does not happen either, and he reports about himself that he stood on such-and-such day to kill him and on another day to honor him, the two standings are distinguished, not by regard to the standing, for it is one, nor by regard to the one standing, for he is one reality, but they are distinguished by that for the sake of which the standing was done. Likewise, whoever stands intending by his standing to honor the king, and stands intending by his standing to honor some commoner, one of them is distinguished from the other in the manner of the deed. But the relation of the Generous Allah to idols is above the relation of kings to commoners; so the deed done for idols is not good. Then, if it happens that someone intends by his deed the face of Allah, exalted is He, yet at the same time worships idols, his deed is not good, because what he did for the sake of Allah is the same as what he did for the carved idol, so there is no glorification.

The second aspect: idlal is making it perishable, and its reality is that when he disbelieves and performs bowing and prostration to stones and wood, he has left himself no dignity, and his act does not remain considered because of his disbelief. This is like one who serves before a guard or groom when he stands up: the sultan does not count his standing as honor because of his lowliness; likewise the disbeliever. As for the believer, to the degree that he is proud before other than Allah, his glorification of Allah becomes manifest, like the king who does not submit to anyone; if at some time he submits to one of the kings, his greatness becomes evident through it.

The third aspect: "adalla" means he neglected it and left it aside, as one says: "adalla his camel" when he leaves it unfettered so that it is lost.

Then, when Allah, exalted is He, had explained the condition of the disbelievers, He explained the condition of the believers.

فَقالَ: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ وآمَنُوا بِما نُزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ وهو الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّهِمْ كَفَّرَ عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ وأصْلَحَ بالَهُمْ﴾. وفِيهِ مَسائِلُ:

**المَسْألَةُ الأُولى:** قَدْ ذَكَرْنا مِرارًا أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى كُلَّما ذَكَرَ الإيمانَ والعَمَلَ الصّالِحَ، رَتَّبَ عَلَيْهِما المَغْفِرَةَ والأجْرَ، كَما قالَ: ﴿فالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ لَهم مَغْفِرَةٌ ورِزْقٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾ [al-Hajj: 50]، وقالَ: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ لَنُكَفِّرَنَّ عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ ولَنَجْزِيَنَّهُمْ﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 70]. وقُلْنا بِأنَّ المَغْفِرَةَ ثَوابُ الإيمانِ، والأجْرَ عَلى العَمَلِ الصّالِحِ، واسْتَوْفَيْنا البَحْثَ فِيهِ في سُورَةِ العَنْكَبُوتِ. فَنَقُولُ هَهُنا: جَزاءُ ذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُ: ﴿كَفَّرَ عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 2]، إشارَةٌ إلى ما يُثِيبُ عَلى الإيمانِ، وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿وأصْلَحَ بالَهُمْ﴾ إشارَةٌ إلى ما يُثِيبُ عَلى العَمَلِ الصّالِحِ.

**المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ:** قالَتِ المُعْتَزِلَةُ (al-Mu'tazila, the Mu'tazilites): تَكْفِيرُ السَّيِّئاتِ مُرَتَّبٌ عَلى الإيمانِ والعَمَلِ الصّالِحِ، فَمَن آمَنَ ولَمْ يَفْعَلِ الصّالِحاتِ يَبْقى في العَذابِ خالِدًا. فَنَقُولُ: لَوْ كانَ كَما ذَكَرْتُمْ لَكانَ الإضْلالُ مُرَتَّبًا عَلى الكُفْرِ والصَّدِّ، فَمَن يَكْفُرُ لا يَنْبَغِي أنْ تُضَلَّ أعْمالُهُ. أوْ نَقُولُ: قَدْ ذَكَرْنا أنَّ اللَّهَ رَتَّبَ أمْرَيْنِ عَلى أمْرَيْنِ، فَمَن آمَنَ كَفَّرَ سَيِّئاتِهِ، ومَن عَمِلَ صالِحًا أصْلَحَ بالَهُ. أوْ نَقُولُ: أيُّ مُؤْمِنٍ يَتَصَوَّرُ أنَّهُ غَيْرُ آتٍ بِالصّالِحاتِ، بِحَيْثُ لا يَصْدُرُ عَنْهُ صَلاةٌ ولا صِيامٌ ولا صَدَقَةٌ ولا إطْعامٌ؟ وعَلى هَذا فَقَوْلُهُ: (وعَمِلُوا) عَطْفُ المُسَبِّبِ عَلى السَّبَبِ، كَما قُلْنا في قَوْلِ القائِلِ: أكَلْتُ كَثِيرًا وشَبِعْتُ.

**المَسْألَةُ الثّالِثَةُ:** قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وآمَنُوا بِما نُزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ﴾ مَعَ أنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ﴾ أفادَ هَذا المَعْنى، فَما الحِكْمَةُ فِيهِ وكَيْفَ وجْهُهُ؟ فَنَقُولُ: أمّا وجْهُهُ فَبَيانُهُ مِن وُجُوهٍ:

الأوَّلُ: قَوْلُهُ: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ أيْ: بِاللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ، وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿وآمَنُوا بِما نُزِّلَ﴾ أيْ: بِجَمِيعِ الأشْياءِ الوارِدَةِ في كَلامِ اللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ، تَعْمِيمٌ بَعْدَ أُمُورٍ خاصَّةٍ، وهو حَسَنٌ، تَقُولُ: خَلَقَ اللَّهُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ وكُلَّ شَيْءٍ، إمّا عَلى مَعْنى: وكُلَّ شَيْءٍ غَيْرَ ما ذَكَرْنا، وإمّا عَلى العُمُومِ بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ الخُصُوصِ.

الثّانِي: أنْ يَكُونَ المَعْنى: آمَنُوا، وآمَنُوا مِن قَبْلُ بِما نُزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ، وهو الحَقُّ المُعْجِزُ الفارِقُ بَيْنَ الكاذِبِ والصّادِقِ، يَعْنِي: آمَنُوا أوَّلًا بِالمُعْجِزِ، وأيْقَنُوا بِأنَّ القُرْآنَ لا يَأْتِي بِهِ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ، فَآمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ. والواوُ لِلْجَمْعِ المُطْلَقِ، ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ المُتَأخِّرُ ذِكْرًا مُتَقَدِّمًا وُقُوعًا، وهَذا كَقَوْلِ القائِلِ: آمَنَ بِهِ، وكانَ الإيمانُ بِهِ واجِبًا. أوْ يَكُونُ بَيانًا لِإيمانِهِمْ، كَأنَّهم ﴿وآمَنُوا بِما نُزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ﴾ أيْ: آمَنُوا وآمَنُوا بِالحَقِّ، كَما يَقُولُ القائِلُ: خَرَجْتُ وخَرَجْتُ مُصِيبًا، أيْ: وكانَ خُرُوجِي جَيِّدًا حَيْثُ نَجَوْتُ مِن كَذا ورَبِحْتُ كَذا. فَكَذَلِكَ لَمّا قالَ: آمَنُوا، بَيَّنَ أنَّ إيمانَهم كانَ بِما أمَرَ اللَّهُ وأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ، لا بِما كانَ باطِلًا مِن عِنْدِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ.

الثّالِثُ: ما قالَهُ أهْلُ المَعْرِفَةِ (ahl al-ma'rifa, the people of gnosis)، وهو أنَّ العِلْمَ العَمَلُ والعَمَلَ العِلْمُ. فَالعِلْمُ يَحْصُلُ لِيُعْمَلَ بِهِ، لِما جاءَ: إذا عَمِلَ العالِمُ العَمَلَ الصّالِحَ عَلِمَ ما لَمْ يَكُنْ يَعْلَمُ. فَيَعْلَمُ الإنْسانُ مَثَلًا قُدْرَةَ اللَّهِ بِالدَّلِيلِ، وعِلْمَهُ وأمْرَهُ، فَيَحْمِلُهُ الأمْرُ عَلى الفِعْلِ، ويَحُثُّهُ عَلَيْهِ عِلْمُهُ، فَعِلْمُهُ بِحالِهِ، وقُدْرَتُهُ عَلى ثَوابِهِ وعِقابِهِ. فَإذا أتى بِالعَمَلِ الصّالِحِ عَلِمَ مِن أنْواعِ مَقْدُوراتِ اللَّهِ ومَعْلُوماتِ اللَّهِ تَعالى ما لَمْ يَعْلَمْهُ أحَدٌ إلّا بِإطْلاعِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وبِكَشْفِهِ ذَلِكَ لَهُ، فَيُؤْمِنُ. وهَذا هو المَعْنِيُّ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ السَّكِينَةَ في قُلُوبِ المُؤْمِنِينَ لِيَزْدادُوا إيمانًا مَعَ إيمانِهِمْ﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. فَإذا آمَنَ المُكَلَّفُ بِمُحَمَّدٍ بِالبُرْهانِ وبِالمُعْجِزَةِ، وعَمِلَ صالِحًا، حَمَلَهُ عِلْمُهُ عَلى أنْ يُؤْمِنَ بِكُلِّ ما قالَهُ مُحَمَّدٌ، ولَمْ يَجِدْ في نَفْسِهِ شَكًّا. ولِلْمُؤْمِنِ في المَرْتَبَةِ الأُولى أحْوالٌ، وفي المَرْتَبَةِ الأخِيرَةِ أحْوالٌ. أمّا في الإيمانِ بِاللَّهِ، فَفي الأوَّلِ يَجْعَلُ اللَّهَ مَعْبُودًا، وقَدْ يَقْصِدُ غَيْرَهُ في حَوائِجِهِ، فَيَطْلُبُ الرِّزْقَ مِن زَيْدٍ وعَمْرٍو، ويَجْعَلُ أمْرًا سَبَبًا لِأمْرٍ. وفي الأخِيرَةِ يَجْعَلُ اللَّهَ مَقْصُودًا، ولا يَقْصِدُ غَيْرَهُ، ولا يَرى إلّا مِنهُ سِرَّهُ وجَهْرَهُ، فَلا يُنِيبُ إلى شَيْءٍ في شَيْءٍ. فَهَذا هو الإيمانُ الآخِرُ بِاللَّهِ، وذَلِكَ الإيمانُ الأوَّلُ.
وأمّا في النَّبِيِّ ﷺ، فَيَقُولُ أوَّلًا: هو صادِقٌ فِيما يَنْطِقُ، ويَقُولُ آخِرًا: لا نُطْقَ لَهُ إلّا بِاللَّهِ، ولا كَلامَ يُسْمَعُ مِنهُ إلّا وهو مِنَ اللَّهِ. فَهو في الأوَّلِ يَقُولُ بِالصِّدْقِ ووُقُوعِهِ مِنهُ، وفي الثّانِي يَقُولُ بِعَدَمِ إمْكانِ الكَذِبِ مِنهُ؛ لِأنَّ حاكِيَ كَلامِ الغَيْرِ لا يُنْسَبُ إلَيْهِ الكَذِبُ، ولا يُمْكِنُ إلّا في نَفْسِ الحِكايَةِ، وقَدْ عَلِمَ هو أنَّهُ حاكٍ عَنْهُ كَما قالَهُ. وأمّا في المَرْتَبَةِ الأُولى، فَيَجْعَلُ الحَشْرَ مُسْتَقْبَلًا والحَياةَ العاجِلَةَ حالًا، وفي المَرْتَبَةِ الأخِيرَةِ يَجْعَلُ الحَشْرَ حالًا والحَياةَ الدُّنْيا ماضِيًا، فَيُقَسِّمُ حَياةَ نَفْسِهِ في كُلِّ لَحْظَةٍ، ويَجْعَلُ الدُّنْيا كُلَّها عَدَمًا لا يَلْتَفِتُ إلَيْها ولا يُقْبِلُ عَلَيْها.

**المَسْألَةُ الرّابِعَةُ:** قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وآمَنُوا بِما نُزِّلَ عَلى مُحَمَّدٍ﴾ هو في مُقابَلَةِ قَوْلِهِ في حَقِّ الكُفّارِ: ﴿وصَدُّوا﴾؛ لِأنّا بَيَّنّا في وجْهٍ أنَّ المُرادَ بِهِمْ: صَدُّوا عَنِ اتِّباعِ مُحَمَّدٍ ﷺ. وهَذا حَثٌّ عَلى اتِّباعِ مُحَمَّدٍ ﷺ، فَهم صَدُّوا أنْفُسَهم عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ، وهو مُحَمَّدٌ عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ وما أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ، وهَؤُلاءِ حَثُّوا أنْفُسَهم عَلى اتِّباعِ سَبِيلِهِ. لا جَرَمَ حَصَلَ لِهَؤُلاءِ ضِدُّ ما حَصَلَ لِأُولَئِكَ، فَأضَلَّ اللَّهُ حَسَناتِ أُولَئِكَ، وسَتَرَ عَلى سَيِّئاتِ هَؤُلاءِ.

**المَسْألَةُ الخامِسَةُ:** قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وهُوَ الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾. هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أنْ يَكُونَ ﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ وصْفًا فارِقًا، كَما يُقالُ: رَأيْتُ رَجُلًا مِن بَغْدادَ، فَيَصِيرُ وصْفًا لِلرَّجُلِ فارِقًا بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ مَن يَكُونُ مِنَ المَوْصِلِ وغَيْرِهِ؟ نَقُولُ: لا؛ لِأنَّ كُلَّ ما كانَ مِنَ اللَّهِ فَهو الحَقُّ، فَلَيْسَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن رَبِّهِمْ، بَلْ قَوْلُهُ: (مِن رَبِّهِمْ) خَبَرٌ بَعْدَ خَبَرٍ، كَأنَّهُ قالَ: وهو الحَقُّ وهو مِن رَبِّهِمْ. أوْ إنْ كانَ وصْفًا فارِقًا، فَهو عَلى مَعْنى أنَّهُ الحَقُّ النّازِلُ مِن رَبِّهِمْ؛ لِأنَّ الحَقَّ قَدْ يَكُونُ مُشاهَدًا، فَإنَّ كَوْنَ الشَّمْسِ مُضِيئَةً حَقٌّ، وهو لَيْسَ نازِلًا مِنَ الرَّبِّ، بَلْ هو عِلْمٌ حاصِلٌ بِطَرِيقٍ يَسَّرَهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى لَنا.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿كَفَّرَ عَنْهم سَيِّئاتِهِمْ وأصْلَحَ بالَهُمْ﴾. أيْ: سَتَرَها. وفِيهِ إشارَةٌ إلى بِشارَةٍ ما كانَتْ تَحْصُلُ بِقَوْلِهِ: أعْدَمَها ومَحاها؛ لِأنَّ مَحْوَ الشَّيْءِ لا يُنْبِئُ عَنْ إثْباتِ أمْرٍ آخَرَ مَكانَهُ، وأمّا السَّتْرُ فَيُنْبِئُ عَنْهُ. وذَلِكَ لِأنَّ مَن يُرِيدُ سَتْرَ ثَوْبٍ بالٍ أوْ وسِخٍ لا يَسْتُرُهُ بِمِثْلِهِ، وإنَّما يَسْتُرُهُ بِثَوْبٍ نَفِيسٍ نَظِيفٍ، ولا سِيَّما المَلِكُ الجَوّادُ، إذا سَتَرَ عَلى عَبْدٍ مِن عَبِيدِهِ ثَوْبَهُ البالِيَ، أمَرَ بِإحْضارِ ثَوْبٍ مِنَ الجِنْسِ العالِي لا يَحْصُلُ إلّا بِالثَّمَنِ الغالِي. فَلَيْسَ هَذا هو السَّتْرَ بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ المَحْبُوبِينَ. وكَذَلِكَ المَغْفِرَةُ، فَإنَّ المَغْفِرَةَ والتَّكْفِيرَ مِن بابٍ واحِدٍ في المَعْنى، وهَذا هو المَذْكُورُ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ يُبَدِّلُ اللَّهُ سَيِّئاتِهِمْ حَسَناتٍ﴾ [al-Furqan: 70]. وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿وأصْلَحَ بالَهُمْ﴾ إشارَةٌ إلى ما ذَكَرْنا مِن أنَّهُ يُبْدِلُها حَسَنَةً. فَإنْ قِيلَ: كَيْفَ تُبَدَّلُ السَّيِّئَةُ حَسَنَةً؟ نَقُولُ: مَعْناهُ أنَّهُ يَجْزِيهِ بَعْدَ سَيِّئاتِهِ ما يَجْزِي المُحْسِنَ عَلى إحْسانِهِ. فَإنْ قالَ: الإشْكالُ باقٍ وبادٍ، وما زالَ بَلْ زادَ، فَإنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى لَوْ أثابَ عَلى السَّيِّئَةِ كَما يُثِيبُ عَنِ الحَسَنَةِ، لَكانَ ذَلِكَ حَثًّا عَلى السَّيِّئَةِ. نَقُولُ: ما قُلْنا إنَّهُ يُثِيبُ عَلى السَّيِّئَةِ، وإنَّما قُلْنا: إنَّهُ يُثِيبُ بَعْدَ السَّيِّئَةِ بِما يُثِيبُ عَلى الحَسَنَةِ، وذَلِكَ حَيْثُ يَأْتِي المُؤْمِنُ بِسَيِّئَةٍ، ثُمَّ يَتَنَبَّهُ ويَنْدَمُ ويَقِفُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَبِّهِ مُعْتَرِفًا بِذَنْبِهِ، مُسْتَحْقِرًا لِنَفْسِهِ، فَيَصِيرُ أقْرَبَ إلى الرَّحْمَةِ مِنَ الَّذِي لَمْ يُذْنِبْ، ودَخَلَ عَلى رَبِّهِ مُفْتَخِرًا في نَفْسِهِ. فَصارَ الذَّنْبُ شَرْطًا لِلنَّدَمِ، والثَّوابُ لَيْسَ عَلى السَّيِّئَةِ، وإنَّما هو عَلى النَّدَمِ. وكَأنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى قالَ: عَبْدِي أذْنَبَ ورَجَعَ إلَيَّ، فَفِعْلُهُ شَيْءٌ، لَكِنَّ ظَنَّهُ بِي حَسَنٌ، حَيْثُ لَمْ يَجِدْ مَلْجَأً غَيْرِي فاتَّكَلَ عَلى فَضْلِي. والظَّنُّ عَمَلُ القَلْبِ، والفِعْلُ عَمَلُ البَدَنِ، واعْتِبارُ عَمَلِ القَلْبِ أوْلى؛ ألا تَرى أنَّ النّائِمَ والمُغْمى عَلَيْهِ لا يُلْتَفَتُ إلى عَمَلِ بَدَنِهِ، والمَفْلُوجُ الَّذِي لا حَرَكَةَ لَهُ يُعْتَبَرُ قَصْدُ قَلْبِهِ؟ ومِثالُ الرُّوحِ والبَدَنِ: راكِبُ دابَّةٍ يَرْكُضُ فَرَسُهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ مَلِكٍ، يَدْفَعُ عَنْهُ العَدُوَّ بِسَيْفِهِ وسِنانِهِ، والفَرَسُ يُلَطِّخُ ثَوْبَ المَلِكِ بِرَكْضِهِ في اسْتِنانِهِ، فَهَلْ يُلْتَفَتُ إلى فِعْلِ الدّابَّةِ مَعَ فِعْلِ الفارِسِ؟ بَلْ لَوْ كانَ الرّاكِبُ فارِغًا، والفَرَسُ يُؤْذِي بِالتَّلْوِيثِ، يُخاطَبُ الفارِسُ بِهِ. فَكَذَلِكَ الرُّوحُ راكِبٌ، والبَدَنُ مَرْكُوبٌ؛ فَإنْ كانَتِ الرُّوحُ مَشْغُولَةً بِعِبادَةِ اللَّهِ وذِكْرِهِ، ويَصْدُرُ مِنَ البَدَنِ شَيْءٌ لا يُلْتَفَتُ إلَيْهِ، بَلْ يُسْتَحْسَنُ مِنهُ ذَلِكَ، ويُزادُ في تَرْبِيَةِ الفَرَسِ الرّاكِضِ، ويُهْجَرُ الفَرَسُ الواقِفُ. وإنْ كانَ غَيْرَ مَشْغُولٍ فَهو مُؤاخَذٌ بِأفْعالِ البَدَنِ.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved followed falsehood, and those who believed followed the truth from their Lord.﴾ That is, that misguidance and nullification happened because of their following falsehood. In this are several issues (masā'il, sing. mas'alah, "question" or "point of discussion"):

The first issue: concerning falsehood (al-bāṭil), there are several meanings.

The first: what cannot possibly exist. This is because they followed a god other than Allah, and a god other than Allah is impossible to exist. This is falsehood and the utmost of falsehood, because falsehood (al-bāṭil) is the non-existent. It is said: "such-and-such nullified (baṭala)," meaning it ceased to exist. The non-existent that cannot possibly exist, cannot be brought into being, and cannot become an existent truth, is in the utmost state of nullity. Based on this, the truth (al-ḥaqq) is that which cannot be made non-existent, and that is Allah, exalted is He. This is because the truth is the existent. It is said: "the matter was verified (taḥaqqaqa)," meaning it came into existence and was established. The existent that cannot be made non-existent is in the utmost state of established reality.

The second: falsehood is Satan, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I shall fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you among them, all together.﴾ [Ṣād: 85] So He made clear that Satan is the one followed, and his followers are the disbelievers and the wicked. Based on this, the truth is Allah, because He, exalted is He, set against the party of Satan the party of Allah.

The third: falsehood is the saying of their great ones (kubarā') and the religion of their fathers, as He, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿Nay, they say: "We found our fathers following a religion, and we are guided in their footsteps."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22] Based on this, the truth is what the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed from Allah.

The fourth: falsehood is everything other than Allah, exalted is He, because falsehood and perishing (al-hālik) have one meaning. And ﴿Everything will perish except His Face.﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 88] Based on this, the truth is also Allah, exalted is He.

The second issue: if someone says: "from their Lord" suits only one of the four aspects, namely our statement that what is meant by the truth is what Allah sent down and what the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed from Allah. But on our statement that the truth is Allah, how is His saying ﴿they followed the truth from their Lord﴾ correct?

We say: on this view, "from their Lord" (min rabbihim) is not connected to "the truth" (al-ḥaqq). Rather, its connection is to His saying, exalted is He, "followed" (ittaba'ū). That is: they followed the command of their Lord; that is, by the grace of Allah or the guidance of their Lord, they followed the truth, which is Allah, glorified is He.

The third issue: if falsehood is the non-existent that cannot possibly exist, how is it possible to follow it? We say: since they used to say, "We only act for the idols, and they are gods, and they will reward us for it," they were, in their own claim, followers, and there is no one followed there.

The fourth issue: concerning the believers He said: ﴿they followed the truth from their Lord﴾, and concerning the disbelievers He said: ﴿they followed falsehood﴾, meaning from their gods or Satan. We say: as for their gods, that is because they have no speech and no intellect, and when Allah makes them speak they deny their act, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will disown your associating﴾ [Fāṭir: 14], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they will be deniers of their worship﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 6]. Allah, exalted is He, approved of their act and confirmed them in it. It is also possible to say that His saying "from their Lord" refers to both matters together, meaning: from their Lord these followed falsehood and those followed the truth, that is, from the decree of their Lord and from the presence of their Lord.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus Allah sets forth parables for people.﴾ In this also are issues:

The first issue: what parable did Allah set forth, such that He says: ﴿Thus Allah sets forth parables for people﴾? We say: there are two views:

One of them: the nullifying of the deeds of the disbelievers and the expiating of the evil deeds of the righteous.

The second: the disbeliever's being a follower of falsehood, and the believer's being a follower of the truth.

It may also bear two other meanings:

One of them: on our statement "from their Lord," that is, from the presence of their Lord these followed falsehood and those followed the truth. We say: this is a parable from which all parables are drawn, for all of it comes from Allah: the misguiding and other than it, the following and other than it.

The second: when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that Allah causes the disbeliever's deed to go astray and Allah expiates the believer's evil deeds, and there was a clear opposition between disbelief and faith, since they are opposites, He drew attention to the fact that the cause is such: that is, misguidance and expiation are not due to the opposition and difference, but due to following the truth and following falsehood. When the cause is known, the two acts may be identical in form and in reality, yet one of them produces the nullifying of deeds and the other produces the expiating of evil deeds, because in one of them there is following of the truth and in the other following of falsehood. For whoever believes outwardly while his heart is full of disbelief, and whoever believes inwardly while his heart is full of faith, their two acts coincide outwardly, yet they differ because of following the truth and following falsehood, and there is no wonder in this. For whoever believes outwardly while concealing disbelief, and whoever disbelieves outwardly under compulsion while his heart is at rest in faith, the two acts differ outwardly. The nullifying of deeds applies to one who displays faith, because following falsehood is on his side. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: disbelief and faith are two like cases in which two rulings are established, and their cause is known, namely following the truth and falsehood. Likewise, know that everything in which the truth is followed is accepted and rewarded, and every matter in which falsehood is followed is rejected and punished. Thus this becomes general in parables. Moreover, we say: His saying "thus" (kadhālika) does not require that there be a parable struck; rather its meaning is that when He, exalted is He, made clear the state of the disbeliever and the nullifying of his deeds, and the state of the believer and the expiating of his evil deeds, and made clear the cause of both, that was the utmost clarification. So He said: "thus" (that is, like this explanation): ﴿Allah sets forth parables for people﴾ and makes clear to them their states.

The second issue: the pronoun in His saying ﴿their parables﴾ (amthālahum) refers to whom? There are two views:

One of them: to all people, as He said: ﴿Allah sets forth parables for people﴾, concerning themselves.

The second: to the two groups mentioned earlier. Its meaning: Allah sets forth for people the parables of the two groups mentioned earlier.

Then God Most High said: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike the necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them﴾, and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: the fa' (so) in His words ﴿So when you meet﴾ calls for an element it is connected to and follows from. What is the connection with what precedes it? We say it has several aspects:

The first: when He explained that God had made the deeds of those who disbelieved go astray, and a person is judged by his deeds, and whoever has no deed is a worthless creature (hamaj), and if he additionally causes harm, his execution becomes good, then: ﴿So when you meet﴾, after it has become clear that they have no sanctity and after their deeds have been nullified, strike their necks.

The second: when the distinction between the two groups and the divergence of the two paths has become clear, and that one of them follows falsehood, and it is the party of Satan, while the other follows truth, and it is the party of the Merciful, fighting becomes due at the time of partisanship. So when you meet them, fight them.

The third: some people say, out of weakness of heart and shortness of vision, that inflicting pain on living beings is oppression and tyranny, especially killing, which is the destruction of a structure. It is answered in refutation of them: since the consideration of deeds is by following truth or falsehood, whoever is killed in the way of God, for the glorification of God's command, receives the same reward as one who prays and fasts. So when you meet those who disbelieve, kill them, and let no compassion for them take hold of you, for that is following the truth, and the consideration is by it, not by the outward form of the act.

The second issue: ﴿ḍarba﴾ (ضَرْبَ) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: strike the striking of necks.

The third issue: What is the wisdom in choosing the striking of the neck over other limbs? We say: when He explained that the believer is not merely defending but is a repeller, since whoever repels an aggressor should not first aim at killing him, but should proceed gradually and strike at non-lethal places, and if he is repelled, that suffices and he does not escalate to destruction, God Most High said: the aim is only to drive them away from the face of the earth and to cleanse the earth of them. And how not, when the earth is a mosque for you, and the polytheists are impure, and a mosque is purified of impurity. Therefore your intention should first be to kill them, unlike repelling an aggressor. The neck is the most evident of the vital places, for cutting the windpipe and the jugular veins entails death, but in battle this is not easily achieved, while the neck is visible in battle, so striking it entails severing the neck, which necessarily results in death, unlike other places, especially in battle. And in His words ﴿you meet﴾ there is an indication of their opposition to the aggressor, for His words ﴿you meet﴾ indicate that the intention comes from their side, unlike our saying "he met you" (laqiyakum). That is why in another place He said: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

The fourth issue: Here He said ﴿striking of the necks﴾ with the verbal noun expressed and the verb omitted, while in al-Anfal He said: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ [al-Anfal: 12] with the verb expressed and the verbal noun omitted. Is there a benefit in this? We say: yes, and we shall show it by introducing a premise: that the primary intention in some surahs may be the occurrence of the act from an agent, and the verbal noun follows it implicitly, since no agent can act without the verbal noun occurring in existence; and the primary intention may be the verbal noun, but it exists only from an agent, so he is commanded to act. An example: if someone says, "I have sworn that I will leave the city," it is said to him, "Then leave." The intention becomes the occurrence of the act from him, and the departure in itself is not the intended object of negation. If it were possible for him to leave without the departure being realized by him, it would not be required of him except that he leave; but among the necessities of departure is that he leave. So if someone says, "The place has become too narrow for me because of the enemies," it is said to him, for example: "Departure means departure, so leave," for departure is what is sought, even if departure were possible without an agent, the purpose would be achieved; but this is impossible, so the act follows. Knowing this, we say: in al-Anfal, the account concerns a battle in which they were present, and the angels were sent down to support those who were present in the battle line, so the occurrence of the act from them is sought, and here the command comes and is not at the time of the fighting, as shown by His words ﴿So when you meet﴾; and the intention is to show that the verbal noun is sought, since the object of command precedes the act, so He said ﴿striking of the necks﴾. In what we have mentioned there is the clarification of another benefit: God Most High said there: ﴿And strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and that is because the time was the time of fighting, so He guided them to the vital place and to other places if they did not strike the vital place. Here, it is not the time of fighting, so He made clear that the intention is killing, and the aim of the Muslim is that.

The fifth issue: (ḥattā) (until) indicates the limit of the command, not the limit of the killing; that is, ﴿until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them﴾, the command to kill ceases and permission remains. Had it indicated the limit of killing, killing would not be permissible at all. Killing is permissible when the one who has been rendered helpless is an aged old man, and what is meant is, for example, when his hands and feet have been cut off, and He forbade killing him.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿So bind them firmly﴾, a command of guidance.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Then either release them as a favour or ransom them﴾, and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: "imma" (either) is for restriction, yet their state after capture is not limited to these two matters; rather killing, enslavement, release and ransom are permissible. We say: this is guidance, so He mentioned the general matter permissible for all peoples, and enslavement is not permissible for captives of the Arabs, for the Prophet ﷺ was among them and did not mention enslavement; as for killing, it is because the apparent meaning of one who is "inflicted with slaughter" is incapacitation; and because killing was mentioned by His words ﴿striking of the necks﴾, so only the two matters remained.

The second issue: manan (release as a favour) and fida'an (ransom) are in the accusative because both are verbal nouns; the implied construction is: "either you grant release as a favour, or you ransom them." The mention of release before ransom indicates the preference of the sanctity of life over the seeking of wealth. Ransom may be wealth, or it may be other captives, or a condition imposed upon them or upon him alone.

The third issue: If we take the verb, namely "you grant" or "you ransom," as having an object, so that we say "either you grant them release or you ransom them," we say: no; because the intention is release and ransom themselves, not directed at them, just as one says, "So-and-so gives and withholds," and one does not say, "He gives Zayd and withholds from ʿUmar," because his purpose is to mention that he is the agent, not to specify the object. Likewise here, the intention is to guide the believers to virtue.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾.

There are two views concerning the connection of (ḥattā):
One: that it connects to the killing, meaning "kill them until it lays down."
The second: that it connects to release and ransom. It may be said that it is connected to ﴿bind firmly﴾; its connection to killing is more evident, though its mention is more remote.

Regarding "burdens" (awzār), there are two views:
One: peace.
The second: sins. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: If the meaning is sin, how can war lay down sin, since sin rests on the combatant? The same question arises regarding weapons, but it is more pressing in the first case. It is said: war lays down burdens not of its own, but lays down the burdens that are upon the combatants and the weapons that are upon them.

The second issue: Is this like His words ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], so that it is as if He had said: "until the nation of war, or the faction of war, lays down its burdens"? We say: this is possible at first glance, but when you consider the meaning deeply you find a difference between them. This is because the intention of His words ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ is war entirely, such that no faction of the factions of disbelief remains in the world that wars against a faction of the factions of Islam. If we said "until the nation of war lays down," it would be permissible that they lay down their weapons and abandon war while it remains in its substance, just as you say, "My dispute has not been settled, but I have abandoned it in these days." When the laying down is ascribed to war, its meaning is that war has ceased.

The third issue: If He had said "until war no longer remains" or "until one flees from war," would the meaning of His words ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ be achieved? We say: no, and the difference between the two expressions, setting aside arrangement, lies in the meaning itself, like the difference between your saying "the dynasty of the Umayyads came to an end" and your saying "no trace of their dominion remained." Without doubt the second is more eloquent. Likewise here, His words ﴿its burdens﴾ mean its traces, for among the burdens of war are its traces.

The fourth issue: When is the time of the laying down of the burdens of war? We say: there are views, whose substance returns to the point that this time is the time when no faction of the factions of Islam and no faction of the factions of disbelief remains. It was said that this is at the fighting of the Dajjal and the descent of ʿIsa, peace be upon him.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾.

Concerning the meaning of "that," there are two views:
One: the matter is that, and the subject is omitted. It may be said: "that is obligatory or prescribed," as one says, "If you do it, then that is so," meaning that is intended and required. Then He clarified that fighting them is not a definite path; rather, had God willed, He would have destroyed them without an army.

His words: ﴿But that He might test some of you by means of others﴾.

That is, but that He might impose it upon you, so that honour is attained for you through His choosing you for this matter. If it is asked: what is the truth of our saying, "obligation is a trial and test," while God knows the secret and what is more hidden? And what is understood from His words ﴿But that He might test some of you by means of others﴾? We say there are several aspects:

The first: that what is meant is that He does that as the act of those who test, that is, as the one who tries and examines does. Among its implications is that God Most High tests in order that the matter may become manifest to others, either to the angels or to people. The truth is that testing, trial and examination are an act by which a matter becomes manifest, which is not definitely determined for intellects when considered, with the intention of its manifestation. Our saying "an act by which a matter becomes manifest" is clearly included in the concept of beginning, because what manifests nothing by its means is not called a trial at all. As for our saying "a matter not definitely determined for intellects," this is because one who strikes a cucumber or a melon with his sword is not said to be testing, since the matter that manifests from it is definite, namely cutting and splitting in two parts. But if one strikes a beast with his sword, it is said that he is tested with his sword, to defend himself, and he may cut it or may not cut it. As for our saying "so that that may become manifest from him," this is because one who strikes a beast with his sword to repel it from himself is not said to be tested, since his striking is not for the manifestation of a definite matter. Knowing this, we say: when God Most High commands us to an act by which a matter not definitely determined manifests—namely either obedience or disobedience in intellects—in order to make that manifest, He is then testing, even though He knows it, because the absence of knowledge is joined in us for our testing. When we are tested, and the absence of knowledge in us persists, we are commanded, and this is not among the necessities of testing. If it is said: the benefit of testing is the attainment of knowledge for the one who tests; so if God Most High is knowing, what benefit is there in it? We say: this is not a question peculiar to testing, for the saying of one who says, "Why did He test?" is like the saying of one who says, "Why did He punish the unbeliever while He is self-sufficient?" and "Why did He create fire burning while He is able to create it such that it benefits and does not harm?" Its answer is: He is not questioned about what He does; and we then say what the earlier scholars said: that it is for the manifestation of the definite matter, and indeed He is God. After this we say: the one who tests has no need for the matter that manifests from the testing, for the one who tests a sword in the case we have mentioned has no need to cut what he tests the sword upon; so that even if he were in need—as we gave the example of repelling a beast with a sword—one does not say he is testing. And His words ﴿But that He might test some of you by means of others﴾ are an indication of the absence of need, confirming His words ﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who are killed in the way of Allah — He will never let their deeds go astray.﴾

It has been read as "qatalū" (they killed) and "qātalū" (they fought), and all of them are suitable to what preceded. As for the one who reads "qatalū" (they killed), then because He said ﴿So strike the necks﴾, meaning "so kill them," He clarified what is for the slayer by His saying ﴿And those who are killed in the way of Allah — He will never let their deeds go astray﴾, as a refutation of the one who claimed that killing is a corruption that is forbidden, since it is the annihilation of one who is honored. So He said: their deed is not like the good deed of the disbeliever, which is nullified; rather it is above the good deeds of the disbeliever. Allah has caused the deeds of the disbelievers to go astray, and He will never cause the deeds of the slayers to go astray. So how could killing be an evil deed?

As for the one who reads "qātalū" (they fought), it is more beneficial and more general in its scope, because it includes whoever strives in killing, whether he is killed or not killed.

As for the one who reads "wa-alladhīna qutilū" in the passive voice, we say: it is suitable to what preceded for several reasons:

The first of them: when He, exalted is He, said ﴿So strike the necks﴾, meaning "fight," and killing is not achieved except by advancing, and fear that the one advancing will be killed prevents him from advancing, He said: Do not fear being killed, for whoever is killed in the way of Allah has a reward and recompense that does not prevent the fighter from fighting, but rather urges him toward it.

The second of them: when He, exalted is He, said ﴿That He may test some of you by means of others﴾, the one tested by something, in every aspect of the visible effect of the testing, is in one of the states: the tempered sword whose value increases if it cuts and decreases if it does not cut. So what is the state of those being tested? He said: if he is killed, then he will not have his deed go astray, and he will be guided, honored, and admitted into Paradise. As for if he kills, then it is not hidden... immediately and eventually. He left its explanation in the case of his being a slayer because it is evident, and He explained his state in the case of his being killed.

The third of them: when He, exalted is He, said ﴿That He may test you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], and a precious thing is not tested by that whose destruction is feared. The keen, sharp, great-value Indian sword is not tested against a hard object that is feared to break it. But the human being is honored; Allah has ennobled him, exalted him, and magnified him. So why did He test him with fighting, which leads to killing and destruction in a frequent, not rare, way? How is this testing good? We say: killing is not destruction with respect to the believer, for it bequeaths eternal life. So if He tests him with fighting, then in the case that he is killed he is honored, and in the case that he is not killed he is honored, if he fights. And if he does not fight, death is inevitable, and he has forfeited for himself the great reward.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So He will never let their deeds go astray﴾, the meaning of "idlal" (causing to go astray) is known. What remains is the difference between the two expressions regarding the disbeliever and the one who misguides. He said "aḍalla" (He caused to go astray) and, regarding the believer who calls to faith, said "lan yuḍilla" (He will never cause to go astray). This is because the fighter is one who calls to faith, since His saying ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ has been mentioned to mean: until no sin remains due to war, which is when the disbeliever submits. So the fighter says: either you submit or you are killed. Thus he is a caller, and the disbeliever is an obstructer, and between them there is contrast and opposition. So He said regarding the disbeliever "aḍalla" in the past tense, and did not say "yuḍillu," as an indication that his deed, wherever it existed, is annihilated, as though it had never existed at all. And He said regarding the believer "fa-lan yuḍilla," and did not say "mā aḍalla," as an indication that his deed, whenever it remains upon him, is recorded for him. So "fa-lan yuḍilla" is for perpetuity, and between them is the utmost difference, just as between the caller and the obstructer is the utmost contrast and opposition.

If it is said: what is the meaning of the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-lan yuḍilla﴾?

Its answer: because in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who are killed﴾ there is the meaning of a condition (shart).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 47, verse 5:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will guide them﴾

If it is read "qutilu" (they were killed) or "qatalu" (they fought), then the guidance is to be understood as referring to both the next world and this world. If it is read "qutilu" (they were killed), then it refers to the Hereafter: "He will guide them" to the path of Paradise without any halting at their graves on the way to the place of their joy.

And His saying: ﴿and He will set their minds at ease﴾.

Its explanation has already been given in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He set their minds at ease﴾. The past and the future tense here refer back to the fact that there, He promised them what He promised them on account of faith and righteous deeds, and that was actually taking place from them, so He informed about the reward with a form that indicates occurrence. Here, He promised them on account of fighting and being killed, so the wording contained something that indicates the future, because His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when you meet﴾ indicates the future, so He said: ﴿and He will set their minds at ease﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He will admit them to Paradise﴾.

It is as if Allah, at the time of their gathering (hashr), guides them to the path of Paradise and clothes them along the way in the robes of honour (khula‘ al-karamah), which is the setting right of their state (islah al-bal): ﴿And He will admit them to Paradise﴾. So it follows the order of occurrence.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿He has made it known to them﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: every person knows his station and his abode, so much so that the people of Paradise will know their places in it better than the people of Jumu‘ah (the Friday assembly) know their homes when they disperse into the land, each one returning to his dwelling. Some have said: the angel appointed over their deeds guides him.

The second interpretation: ﴿He has made it known to them﴾ means He made it good (ṭayyabahā), as in the saying "ṭa‘ām mu‘arraf" (food that has been seasoned/perfumed).

The third interpretation: al-Zamakhshari said: it may be said that "He has made it known to them" means He defined it, from "‘arafa al-dar" and "arafahā", i.e., He delimited it, and its delimitation is in His saying: ﴿a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al ‘Imran: 133]. It may also be said that what is meant is His saying: ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been made to inherit﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72], pointing to it and making it known to them that it is that one. There is another interpretation, which is that its meaning is: ﴿He has made it known to them﴾ before the killing, for the martyr, before his death, has his station in Paradise displayed to him, so he longs for it. A second interpretation: its meaning is ﴿And He will admit them to Paradise﴾, and there is no need to describe it, for He has made it known to them repeatedly and has described it. A third interpretation: it is from the category of announcing a lost item (ta‘rif al-dallah). When Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [at-Tawbah: 111], it is as if He said: whoever takes Paradise and seeks it with his wealth or his self, then the one who was killed heard the announcement, gave what was asked of him for it, and so he was admitted to it.

Then, when He explained the reward and recompense for fighting, He promised them victory in this world as an added encouragement, so that their eagerness to advance would increase. He said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you support Allah, He will support you and make firm your feet﴾.

Regarding Allah's support there are several interpretations. The first: if you support the religion of Allah and His way. The second: if you support the party of Allah and His group. The third: what is meant is the support of Allah in reality. We say: support is the realization of the objective of one of two opponents at the time of striving, and the undertaking to achieve its sign. Thus Satan, the enemy of Allah, strives to realize disbelief and the dominance of the people of faith, while Allah seeks the suppression of disbelief, the destruction of its people, and the annihilation of those who chose association (ishrak) out of their ignorance. So whoever realizes the support of Allah, by realizing His objective, is one for whom you do not say "he realized His will," for the will of Allah is not realized by anyone else, and His objective, according to the People of the Sunnah, is other than His will, since He sought faith from the disbeliever but did not will it; otherwise it would have occurred.

Then He said: ﴿He will support you﴾. If it is asked: what then do you say, since you said that when Allah supports the believers He has realized what He sought, so how can He realize what the servant sought when it is one and the same thing? We say: the believer supports Allah by going out to fight and advancing, and Allah supports him by strengthening him, making his feet firm, and sending the angels who guard him from behind and before him. Then He said, may He be exalted: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, may they have ruin﴾. This is an addition to strengthening their hearts. So they are unable to repel what God has decreed against them of ruin, and in this situation there must be the slipping of the foot and stumbling. He said regarding the believers, ﴿and He will make firm﴾, in the form of a promise, because God is under no obligation to anything. He said regarding them in the form of a supplication, and it is more emphatic than the form of a report from God, because their stumbling is necessary, since the absence of help from their gods is certain to occur, as they have no power. Steadfastness from God is not certain to occur, because He is Powerful and Choosing and does whatever He wills.

His saying: ﴿and He will cause their deeds to go astray﴾ is an indication of the explanation of the difference between their dead and the slain of the Muslims, for He said regarding the slain of the believers: ﴿He will never let their deeds go astray﴾, and He said regarding the dead of the disbelievers: ﴿and He will cause their deeds to go astray﴾. Then God, may He be exalted, explained the cause of what they differed about, saying: ﴿That is because they disliked what God sent down, so He nullified their deeds﴾. In this there are several views.

The first: the intended meaning is the Qur'an. Its aspect is that the manner of righteous action is not known by reason, but is apprehended through the Law (al-shar'), and the Law is in the Qur'an. So when they turned away, they did not know righteous action or how to perform it, so they brought falsehood, and God nullified their deeds.

The second: ﴿they disliked what God sent down﴾ refers to the explanation of monotheism, as God, may He be exalted, said of them: ﴿Shall we really abandon our gods for a mad poet?﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:36), and He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ (Sad 38:5), up to His saying: ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ (Sad 38:7), and He said, may He be exalted: ﴿When God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink﴾ (Al-Zumar 39:45). Its aspect is that shirk nullifies deeds. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿If you associate others with Him, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ (Al-Zumar 39:65). And how could it not be so, when the deed of the polytheist does not occur for the sake of God's Face? So it has no permanence in itself, and no permanence through the permanence of the One to whom the deed belongs, because everything other than the Face of God, may He be exalted, is perishing and nullified.

The third: ﴿they disliked what God sent down﴾ refers to the explanation of the matter of the Hereafter, so they did not work for it, while the world and what is in it and its outcome are false, so God nullified their deeds.

His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them?﴾ In it there is a connection to the third aspect, meaning: that they should look at their condition and know that the world is perishing.

His saying: ﴿God destroyed them﴾, that is, He destroyed upon them the enjoyment of the world, of wealth, children, spouses and bodies.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and for the disbelievers are similar things﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: that the intended meaning is that for them there are similar things in this world, and in that case the intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is those who disbelieve in Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace.

The second: that the intended meaning is that for them there are similar things in the Hereafter, so the intended meaning is those mentioned earlier, as if He were saying: God destroyed them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there are similar things. The feminine pronoun in His saying ﴿similar things﴾ refers back to something, and there are two views on it:

The first: it is what has been mentioned, namely the outcome (al-aqibah).

The second: it is what is understood, namely the punishment (al-uqubah), because the destruction was a punishment for them. If it is said: according to our view, the intended meaning of "for the disbelievers in Muhammad, peace be upon him, are similar things to what was the outcome for those before them", a question arises: the earlier peoples were destroyed by severe calamities such as earthquakes, fires and other things such as winds and the flood, and this was not the case for the people of Muhammad ﷺ. We say: their punishment may be more severe than the punishment of the earlier peoples, because the religion of Muhammad was more manifest through the coming of the prophets, peace be upon them, before him, and their informing about him and warning of him. Moreover, they killed and took captive by their own hands those whom they used to belittle and oppress, and killing by the hand of one's own kind is more painful than destruction by a general cause. And another question: if the pronoun refers to the outcome, how can it have similar things? We say: it may be said that the intended meaning is the punishment which is what the outcome signifies, or the pain upon which the outcome was based.

* * *

Then God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is because God is the mawla (protector) of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no mawla﴾.

The word "that" (dhalika) may refer to the help, and this is the choice of a group, mentioned by al-Wahidi. It may also admit of another meaning, more remote in transmission and closer in reason, which is this: since we have explained that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and for the disbelievers are similar things﴾ is an indication that the people of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, were destroyed by the hands of their own kind, those whom they would not accept sitting with, and this is more painful than destruction by a general cause, He said: "that", i.e., the destruction and humiliation, is due to the fact that God, may He be exalted, is the helper of the believers, while the disbelievers took gods that neither benefit nor harm, and abandoned God, so they have no helper. There is no doubt that whomever God, may He be exalted, helps is able to kill and to take captive, even if he has a thousand helpers, let alone one who has no helper at all.

[Page 45]

When Allah, may He be exalted, described the state of the believers and the disbelievers in this world, He then described their state in the Hereafter. He said: indeed, He admits the believer into Paradise and the disbeliever into the Fire. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Allah often limits the description of Paradise to mention of its rivers, because trees follow rivers and fruits follow trees. Also, water is the source of life for the world, whereas fire is the cause of destruction. For the believer, water is something he looks upon and benefits from; for the disbeliever, fire is something he is tossed about in and harmed by.

The second issue: We have mentioned several times that the particle "min" (from) in His saying ﴿from beneath them the rivers﴾ may be a silah (a connecting or supplementary particle), meaning "rivers flow beneath them." It may also mean that their water does not come to them from another place, so that one would ask, "Where does this river originate?" and the answer is, "From the spring of such-and-such, from beneath the mountain of such-and-such."

The third issue: He said, ﴿and those who disbelieve enjoy themselves﴾. He singled them out for mention, although the believer also has enjoyment of the world and its good things. We say: whoever has a great kingdom and also possesses a small amount of something is not mentioned except in terms of the great kingdom. It is said of a great king, "the owner of such-and-such estate," and one who owns only a little is not mentioned except by it. The believer has the kingdom of Paradise, so the goods of this world are not regarded in his case, whereas the disbeliever has nothing but this world.

Another aspect: for the believer, this world is in every case a prison. Whoever eats in a prison is not described as enjoying himself. If it is asked, "How can this world be a prison when it contains so many good things?" we say: the believer in the Hereafter has prepared good things and honoured companions. Their relation, and the relation of those who are in it, to this world may be made clear by an example. Suppose a man owns an orchard containing every kind of good fruit in the utmost delight, with rivers flowing in the utmost clarity, and mansions and chambers of the utmost loftiness, and his children are in it. He has been absent from them for years, then he turns towards them while they are in it. When he draws near to them, he is detained in a thicket that contains some bitter, astringent fruits and turbid waters, and in which there are many beasts of prey and insects. Is his condition there like that of one imprisoned in a dark well or in a ruined house, or not? And is it permissible to say to him, "Leave what is yours, and content yourself with these fruits and these rivers," or not?

Such is the condition of the believer. As for the disbeliever, his condition is like that of one who is brought forward to be killed and endures it for days in a thicket such as the one we have described. Is he in a garden? The relation of this world to Paradise and to the Fire is less than the example we have given; yet it informs the discerning person of the reality of the matter.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿as cattle eat﴾ may carry several meanings:

First: cattle are concerned only with eating, and so is the disbeliever, whereas the believer eats in order to do righteous deeds and to gain strength for them.

Second: cattle do not draw lessons from what they eat concerning their Creator, and neither does the disbeliever.

Third: cattle are fed so that they will grow fat, while they are unaware of the matter. They do not know that the fatter they become, the closer they come to slaughter and destruction. The disbeliever is likewise. This is consistent with His saying, ﴿and the Fire is their abode﴾.

The fourth issue: concerning the believer He said ﴿indeed, Allah admits﴾ in the form of a promise, and concerning the disbeliever He said ﴿and the Fire is their abode﴾ in a form that indicates desert and entitlement. This is because, as we have mentioned, benevolence does not necessarily have to be owed. Whoever bestows favour upon one who has done nothing to deserve it is generous, whereas whoever punishes without desert is unjust.

Know that this is an indication of the distinction between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the disbelievers, so that he may know that the destruction of the disbelievers and the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) in this world are certain, and that the situation is fitting for the punishment of the disbeliever and the reward of the believer. His saying ﴿upon a clear proof﴾ is a decisive distinction, and His saying ﴿from his Lord﴾ completes it. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 47, verse 15 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾.

When He had explained the difference between the two groups in guidance and misguidance, He explained the difference between them in their return and their final state. Just as He placed "man" (man) before "clear proof" (bayyina) in mention, before one who follows his own desire, He placed the state of the former in its outcome before the state of one whose condition is the opposite of his. In the interpretation there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿The parable of the Garden﴾ requires something to which it is likened. What is it? We say there are several views. The first: the saying of Sibawayh, where he said: "The mathal (parable) is the description (wasf), its meaning being the description of the Garden." That does not require a thing to which it is likened. On this view there are two possibilities. One of them: the predicate is omitted and "the parable of the Garden" is the subject, its implied sense being "in what We have related is the parable of the Garden," and then he resumes and says: "in it are rivers." Similarly, in Surah al-Ra'd, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Baqara: 25] is the beginning of an explanation.

The second possibility: "in it are rivers" and His saying "flowing beneath them" is the predicate, as one says: "Describe Zayd to me," and the speaker says: "Zayd is red, short." The second view: the mathal is an addition, and the implied sense is: the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised, in it are rivers.

The second view: here the thing likened to is omitted and not mentioned, and this admits of two sayings. One of them: al-Zajjaj said, where he said: "The parable of the Garden" is a Garden through which flow ﴿rivers in it﴾, as one says: "The likeness of Zayd is a tall, dark man," mentioning the very attributes of Zayd in an indefinite man, who in reality is none other than Zayd.

The second of the two sayings is that its meaning is: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ is a wondrous parable, or a great thing, or something similar. On this view, His saying ﴿in it are rivers﴾ is a new statement confirming our words: "a wondrous parable."

The third view: the thing likened to is mentioned, and this is the saying of al-Zamakhshari, where he said: ﴿Like one who abides in the Fire﴾ [Muhammad: 15] is likened to it by way of denial. In that case it is like the saying of one who says: "The movements or the characters of Zayd are like those of 'Amr." Likewise on one of the two interpretations: either as "like the movements of 'Amr," or as "Zayd in his movements is like 'Amr." So too here, as if He, Exalted is He, said: "The parable of the Garden is like one who abides in the Fire." This is the furthest that the saying of al-Zamakhshari can be established. On this view His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in it are rivers﴾ and what follows it are parenthetical clauses placed between the subject and the predicate, as one says: "The likeness of Zayd, in him is manliness, and with him is knowledge, and for him is the origin of 'Amr."

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste has not changed, and rivers of wine, delightful to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey.﴾

He chose rivers from among the four kinds, and this is because a drink is either drunk for its taste, or drunk for a matter not returning to taste. If it is for taste, the tastes are nine: bitter, salty, pungent, sour, astringent, contracting, insipid, sweet, and fatty. The most delightful of them is the sweet, but the sweetest of things is honey, so He mentioned it. As for the fattiest of things, it is oil; but fattiness when it is pure is not pleasant for eating or drinking, for oil is not eaten or drunk, as is generally the case. As for milk, it contains the fat that exists in other things, and it is good for eating, and by it animals are first nourished, so Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned it. As for what is drunk not for a matter returning to taste, it is water and wine. For in wine there is a matter for which the drinker drinks it, while it is disagreeable in taste by the agreement of those who drink it and the certainty of that by transmission. Then He stripped each of the four things of the attributes of deficiency which they have and by which this world is altered. Water changes; it is said: "the water became stagnant" (asana al-ma'u ya'sanu), on the pattern of amina yamanu, so it is asin (stagnant). Milk becomes stagnant when it remains a time, and its taste changes. Wine is disliked by the drinker at the time of drinking. Honey is mixed with particles of wax, and many bees die in it. Then Allah, Exalted is He, combined the two kinds: He mentioned water which is drunk not for taste, and it is of general drinking, and joined to it milk which is drunk for its taste, and it is of general drinking, since there is no one whose drink is not milk. Then He mentioned wine, which is drunk not for taste, and it is of little drinking, and joined to it honey, which is drunk for taste, and it is of little drinking. If it is said: honey is not drunk, we say: the sherbet of julab was made only from honey and sugar in recent times. Do you not see that sikanjabin is from "sirka wa anguban," which is vinegar and honey in Persian, just as its extraction was originally from vinegar and honey, and sugar was not known until a later time. And because "honey" is a name applied to other than bee honey, so that one says "bee honey" to distinguish it. And Allah knows best.

Second issue: He said of wine: ﴿delightful to the drinkers﴾, and He did not say of milk "whose taste has not changed for the eaters," nor of honey "purified for the beholders." This is because delight varies with the differences of persons, for a food may be enjoyed by one person and loathed by another. So He said: ﴿delightful to the drinkers﴾ in their entirety. And because wine is disagreeable in taste, He said "delightful," meaning that there is no disliking of taste in the wine of the Hereafter. As for taste and colour, they do not vary with the differences among people, for sweet, sour, and other tastes are perceived by everyone in the same way, but some people may loathe it and others find it delightful, while all agree that it has one taste; and likewise with colour. So there was no need for an explicit statement of generality. His saying "delightful" (ladhdha) may bear two meanings. One of them: it is the feminine of ladhdh, as one says: a delicious food (ta'am ladhdh) and delicious foods (at'ima ladhdhatun wa ladhidha).

The second: that it is a description by the very meaning, not by a derived form, as one says of a forbearing man: "he is wholly forbearance," and of a wise man: "he is wholly wisdom."

Its shade is the mercy of Allah and His forgiveness, where no heat or cold touches them.

Third issue: The God-fearing enter only after forgiveness, so how can there be for them therein forgiveness? We answer: the response to this is from two aspects. The first: it is not necessary that the meaning be "for them forgiveness from their Lord therein," but it is a conjunction upon His saying "for them" (lahum), as if He, Exalted is He, said: "For them are the fruits therein, and for them is forgiveness before entering it."

The second: that the meaning be "for them therein is forgiveness," that is, the obligation is lifted from them, so they eat without reckoning, unlike in this world, where fruits come with reckoning or punishment. And another aspect: the one who eats in this world is never free of an unpleasant result, such as sickness or the need to relieve oneself. So He said: ﴿And for them therein is of every fruit, and forgiveness﴾, meaning there is no ugliness upon the eater; rather, his ugly matters are covered and forgiven. I derived this from the teachers in our lands, for they train children to say, at the time of their need to pass urine or the like: "O teacher, may God forgive you," so the teacher understands that they are asking permission to go out to relieve their need, and he grants it to them. So I said to myself: its meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, in Paradise, forgave the one who eats; and in this world, because eating has consequences and necessary accompaniments, the teacher understands from their words their need.

Is this sound or not? We say: if we look at the wording, it can be made sound with forced effort; if we look at the meaning, it is not sound except by returning it to what we mentioned. As for making it sound: by omitting "like" the second time, or making it an apposition to the preceding, or by supposing an elided conjunction that conjoins "like one who abides" to "like one to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive," or to "like one who abides in the Fire." As for the method of apposition, it is corrupt, for otherwise reliance would be on the second, so that it would be as if He said: "Is one who is upon a clear proof like one who abides?" and that is an unseemly comparison, and the speech of God is exalted above that. The same applies to supposing an elided conjunction, for the conjoined also becomes independent in the comparison. This condition does not apply to conjunction with *wa* (and): one may say, with *wa*, "The pilgrims came, and I did not know," but this is not permissible with *ḥattā*. Or it is that they do not understand, although they listen and ask for repetition. The second matter is suited by His saying: ﴿Thus God sets a seal upon the hearts of the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:101]. The first is confirmed by His saying: ﴿And when they are alone with their devils, they say, "We are with you; we are only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14]. The second is confirmed by His saying: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." * * *

Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts God has set a seal, and they followed their desires﴾.

That is, they abandoned following the truth, either because of a lack of understanding or because of not listening in order to benefit, and they followed its opposite.

Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And those who were guided, He increased them in guidance and gave them their taqwa﴾.

When God had made clear that the hypocrite listens but does not benefit, and asks for repetition but does not gain understanding, He showed that the state of the believer who is guided is the opposite of this: he listens and understands, and acts on what he knows, whereas the hypocrite asks for repetition and the guided one explains and repeats. The second is cutting off the excuse of the hypocrite and making clear that his way is blameworthy. For if he were to say, "I did not understand it because of its obscurity and because it is enigmatic," the reply would be, "That is not so, for the guided one understood it and drew out its implications and consequences." That is due to blindness of the hearts, not to the obscurity of what is sought.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 47, verses 18–19:**

*﴿So do they wait for anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly? But already have come its portents.﴾*

This means: the disbelievers and the hypocrites await nothing but the Hour. That is because the proofs have been established and the matters have become clear, yet they have not believed. Therefore, faith is not expected from them except at the establishing of the Hour. This is of the type of *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, a grammatical construction in which the substitute includes or implies the thing substituted) with the construction being: they do not await anything but the Hour, its coming upon them suddenly.

[p. 53]

It was also recited: *﴿So do they wait for anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them?﴾*, as a conditional (*ash-shart*), whose answer is: *"Their remembrance will not benefit them."* This is indicated by the words of the Exalted: *﴿Then how for them, when their reminder has come to them?﴾*. We have already mentioned that the Resurrection was named "the Hour" (*as-sa'a*) because of the momentousness of the events that occur in it, such as the resurrection, the gathering, and the reckoning.

His words: *﴿But already have come its portents﴾* may have two interpretations.

The first: it is to show the extent of their obstinacy. Its clarification is that when the proofs became manifest and they did not believe, nothing remained except the faith of despair, which occurs at the establishing of the Hour. But its portents have appeared, so they should have believed, yet they did not believe. Thus they are in the depths of corruption and the utmost obstinacy.

The second: it serves to console the hearts of the believers. As if the Exalted, when He said *﴿So do they wait?﴾*, implied their punishment, and the Hour is regarded as far off by the common people. So it is as if someone said: "When is the Hour?" Then it is said: *"But already have come its portents,"* like His words: *﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾* (al-Qamar: 1).

The *ashrat* (portents) are the signs. The commentators said: they are like the splitting of the moon and the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him). It may also be said that the meaning of the portents is the clear proofs that demonstrate the possibility of the gathering, such as the creation of man at the beginning and the creation of the heavens and the earth, as the Exalted said: *﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾* (Ya-Sin: 81). The first is the (more established) interpretation.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: *﴿Then how for them, when their reminder has come to them?﴾*, meaning: remembrance will not benefit them, since repentance will not be accepted and faith will not be counted. The intended meaning is: how will their condition be when their reminder comes to them? The meaning of that may be His words: *﴿This is your Day which you were promised﴾* (al-Anbiya: 103), and *﴿This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny﴾* (as-Saffat: 21), so they will be reminded of it for regret. Likewise His words: *﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾* (az-Zumar: 71).

[p. 54]

*﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women. And Allah knows of your movement and your resting place.﴾*

For the explanation of the connection (*al-munasabah*) there are several aspects.

The first: when He said *﴿But already have come its portents﴾*, He said *﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾*, which comes with the Hour, as the Exalted said: *﴿The imminent [Hour] has drawn near. None besides Allah can disclose it﴾* (an-Najm: 57–58).

The second: *﴿But already have come its portents﴾*, while it is still to come. As if someone said: "When is this?" So He said: *﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾*. Do not occupy yourself with it, but occupy yourself with what is incumbent upon you of seeking forgiveness, and be at every time prepared for meeting it. Consistent with this is His words: *﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾*.

The third: *﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾* benefits you. If it is said: the Prophet (peace be upon him) already knew this, so what is the meaning of the command? We say, regarding this, in two aspects:

The first: remain upon what you are upon of knowledge, like the saying of one speaking to a sitter who wants to stand: "Sit," meaning: do not stand.

The second: the address is to the Prophet (peace be upon him), while the intended audience is his people. The pronoun in *annahu* (that He) refers to the matter (*li-sh-sha'n*). The sense of this is: when he (peace be upon him) called the people to faith and they did not believe, and nothing remained that would move them to faith except the manifestation of the matter of resurrection and rising, and that was something that grieved the Prophet (peace be upon him), He consoled his heart and said: you are complete in yourself and you complete others. If a people does not become complete through you, it is because Allah the Exalted did not intend good for them. So you, in yourself, act by your knowledge, and your knowledge is that you know that Allah is One, and you seek forgiveness. And you, by the praise of Allah, are one who completes, you complete the believing men and believing women, and you seek forgiveness for them. Thus the two qualities have been attained for you. So remain upon what you are upon, and let not their disbelief grieve you.

This means: the disbelievers and the hypocrites await nothing but the Hour. That is because the proofs have been established and the matters have become clear, yet they have not believed. Therefore, faith is not expected from them except at the establishing of the Hour. This is of the type of *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, a grammatical construction in which the substitute includes or implies the thing substituted) with the construction being: they do not await anything but the Hour, its coming upon them suddenly.

Then Allah the Exalted sent down a surah in which there is fighting, for it is the most arduous of obligations. His saying: ﴿a clear surah﴾ has several interpretations:

First: a surah that has not been abrogated (naskh). Second: a surah containing expressions whose literal meanings are intended, unlike His saying: ﴿The All-Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] and His saying: ﴿in what I neglected concerning Allah﴾ [az-Zumar: 56]. Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible that the meaning be "so obedience is more fitting for them", i.e., obedience is more fitting for them.

This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "They say: obedience and fair speech."

This accords with the meaning of Ubayy's reading, as if He were saying: at the beginning of the matter they said "We hear and obey," and at the end of the matter they opposed and broke their promise. He attributed resolve (al-'azm) to the matter, while resolve belongs to the one in charge of the matter; its meaning is: "when the one in charge of the matter resolves." This is the statement of az-Zamakhshari. It may also be said that this is a metaphor, like our saying: "The matter has come and turned away," for the matter at first is expected not to occur, but when it casts its shadow and the one who dislikes it is unable to annul it, it has occurred; so He said "resolved." And according to our statement, ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾ is better for them and more excellent; so its meaning is: ﴿if they had been true﴾ in their faith and in following the Messenger, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾.
