This verse contains an allusion to the invalidity of a statement they made, namely that they used to say: "How can we fight, when killing is corruption and the Arabs are among our kin and tribes?" Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you turn away﴾, nothing from you will occur except corruption in the land, for you kill whomever you are able to and plunder him, and fighting is taking place among you. Is not your killing of daughters corruption and severing of kinship? So your pretext for that is not valid, especially since it opposes what Allah commanded; and this is obedience. There are issues regarding this:

The first issue: regarding the use of ʿasā (perhaps/it may be) there are three positions. The first: using it in the form of a past-tense verb with a subject, as you say: ʿasā Zayd, ʿasaynā, ʿasaw, ʿasaytu, ʿasaytumā, ʿasaytum, ʿasat, ʿasatā.

The second: it is used in the form of a verb with an object, as you say: ʿasāhu, ʿasāhumā, ʿasāka, ʿasākumā, ʿasānī, ʿasānā.

The third: it is used without anything attached to it, as you say: ʿasā Zayd yakhruju, ʿasā anta takhruju, ʿasā anā akhruju. Each has a basis, but what the speech of Allah is upon is more appropriate. That is because ʿasā is among the rigid (jāmid) verbs, and the attachment of the subject to the verb is more appropriate than the attachment of the object, because the subject is like a part of the verb; for this reason it is not permitted in it to have four consecutive moving letters in a phrase like the speaker's "nuṣirtu," whereas it is permitted in a phrase like their saying "naṣarakа". Also, every verb has a subject, whether intransitive or transitive, whereas the direct object is not like that. So ʿasayta and ʿasāka are like ʿaṣayta and ʿaṣāka in attaching the subject to the verb and the direct object. As for the saying of whoever said "ʿasā anta taqūmu" and "ʿasā an aqūma," it is inferior to what we mentioned, because of the prolixity it contains.

The second issue: the interrogative is for emphatic confirmation, for if He had said as a report: ﴿you may well sever﴾, the addressee could deny it; but when it is stated in the form of a question, it is as if He says: "I ask you about this, and you cannot answer except with 'no' or 'yes', so it is established by you and by me."

The third issue: ʿasā indicates expectation, and Allah is knowing of everything; so we say about it what we said about laʿalla. And regarding His saying ﴿that We may test them﴾ [al-Kahf: 7], some people said: He acts toward you as one who hopes, tests and anticipates; and others said: everyone who looks at them anticipates that from them; but we said: it is to be taken literally. That is because when an act is possible in itself, looking at it does not necessitate a matter; rather, the matter may occur from it at times and not occur from it at other times, so the act is for that matter sought by way of hope, whether the doer knows the matter will occur from him or does not know it. An example: one who sets a net to catch game—it is said he anticipates that; if he came to know by the report of a truthful source that the game will fall into it, or by another means, he still does not depart from anticipation. The only thing is that in the observable case we do not attain knowledge of what we anticipate, so it is supposed that the absence of knowledge is necessary for the one who anticipates; but that is not so. Rather, the one who anticipates is the one who awaits a matter that is not necessarily bound to occur, merely by his regard for that matter, whether or not he has knowledge of it.

His saying ﴿if you turn away﴾ has two possibilities: One: it is from wilāya (authority), meaning: if you take up authority and people come under your command, you will cause corruption and sever kinship. The second: it is from tawallī, which is turning away (i'rāḍ), and this accords with what we mentioned, i.e., you used to leave off fighting and say that in it is corruption and severing of kinship because the disbelievers are our relatives; so nothing from you will occur except that, when you fight over the slightest thing, as was the custom of the Arabs.

The first: its wording is confirmed by the reading of ʿAlī (ʿalayhi al-salām), "tuwuillitum," i.e., if rulers who are oppressive, harsh and tyrannical take charge over you, and you walk beneath their banner and cause corruption by their corruption and sever your kinship; while the Prophet (ﷺ) commands you only to reform and maintain kinship. So why do you hold back from fighting and distance yourselves in misguidance?

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has deafened them and blinded their sight.﴾

This is a reference to those mentioned earlier among the hypocrites, whom Allah has distanced from Himself or from good. "So He has deafened them" means they do not hear the clear speech, "and blinded them" means they do not follow the straight path. In this there is a fine order (tartib hasan), because they listened to the speech of knowledge (al-kalam al-'ilmi) and did not understand it; so with respect to it they are deaf, which Allah has made them to be. When they were commanded to act, they abandoned it and gave as their reason that it is corruption and severing of the ties of kinship (qat' al-rahim), yet they used to engage in it when they were forbidden from it, so they did not look at their own state in it. They abandoned following the Prophet (ﷺ), who commands them to reform and to maintain the ties of kinship. Had someone who commanded corruption and the severing of kinship called them, they would have followed him. So they are blind, which Allah has made them to be.

This is because the eye is the instrument of sight; if it suffers a calamity, seeing does not occur. The ear, if it suffers a calamity such as cutting or uprooting, does not hear speech, because the ear was created and within it were created convolutions (ta'arij) so that the moving air would collect in it, and it would not strike the ear canal (al-sima') violently, thereby harming it as a loud sound harms. So He said "(deafened them)" without mentioning the ear. And He said "and blinded their sight" with mention of the eye, because here al-basar carries the meaning of the eye, and for this reason He made it plural as al-absar; had it been a verbal noun (masdar), it would not have been pluralized. So He did not mention the ear, since it has no role in deafness, whereas the eye has a role in seeing; rather it is the whole matter. What indicates this is that when calamity was attributed to the ear in other places, He named it waqr (heaviness), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And in our ears is heaviness﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and He said: ﴿As if in his ears was heaviness﴾ [Luqman: 7]. Waqr is less than complete deafness (al-samm), and likewise tarash (partial deafness).

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾

We shall mention its tafsir (exegesis) in several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah).

**The first issue:** When God, exalted is He, said, ﴿So He deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾, how could they reflect upon the Qur'an? Then He said, ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ This is like the saying of someone to a blind man, "See!" and to a deaf man, "Listen!" We say: the answer to this has three aspects, arranged so that some are better than others.

The first: imposing what cannot be borne is permissible. God commanded the one whom He knew would not believe to believe. Likewise, it is permissible that He blinds them and reproaches them for abandoning reflection.

The second: the meaning of His saying, ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ is "people."

The third: we say that this verse came to confirm the meaning of the preceding verse. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Those are the ones whom God has cursed﴾, meaning He distanced them from Him, or from truthfulness, or from goodness, or from other good matters. ﴿So He deafened them﴾, so they do not hear the reality of speech, ﴿and blinded them﴾, so they do not follow the path of Islam. Thus they are between two states. Either they do not reflect upon the Qur'an and so they are distanced from it, because God has cursed them and distanced them from good and truthfulness, and the Qur'an is of the highest category of these, indeed the most noble kind. Or they do reflect, but its meanings do not enter their hearts because the hearts are locked. The sense is: ﴿Will they not reflect upon the Qur'an﴾ because they are accursed and rejected, or ﴿are there locks upon hearts﴾ so that they reflect but do not understand? On this view we do not need to say that the particle ʾam (أم) means "rather" (بل). Rather it stays in its own sense of interrogation, positioned in the middle of the speech, and the interrogative hamza (الهمزة) has taken its place at the beginning, and ʾam has entered upon the hearts, which are in the middle of the speech.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿upon hearts﴾, in indefinite form (al-tankir). What is its benefit? We say: al-Zamakhshari said: it may have two aspects. One is that it indicates that they are described by an attribute, because an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective is more fitting than a definite one. So it is as if He said: "upon hearts that are hard or dark."

The second: that it is partitive (lil-tab'id), as if He said: "upon some of the hearts," because an indefinite noun does not generalize. You say, "Men came to me," and the meaning understood is some; "The men came to me," and the meaning understood is all. We say: the indefiniteness of "hearts" serves to draw attention to the denial that is in the hearts. This is because when the heart knows, it is known, since the heart was created for knowledge. When there is no knowledge in it, it is as if it is not known. This is like the speaker who says of a harmful person, "This is not a human, this is a beast." Likewise one says, "This is not a heart, this is a stone."

Once this is known: the definiteness is either by al-alif wa al-lam (the article) or by idafah (construct). The al-lam is either for definiteness of kind (lil-jins) or for a known referent (lil-'ahd). Taking it as kind is impossible, since not every heart has a lock. Nor can it be a known referent, since that heart should not be called a heart. Or it is by idafah, saying "upon hearts whose locks," and it is for lack of any benefit returning to them, as if they were not theirs. If it is said: He has said, ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] and ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. We say: the locks are more emphatic than the seal, so He omitted the idafah because they derive no benefit at all.

**The third issue:** In His saying, ﴿its locks﴾, with idafah, and He did not say "locks" (aqfal) as He said "hearts" (qulub), because locks were among the affairs of the hearts, so He attributed them to them, as if they were for nothing but them. In general, He did not attribute the hearts to them because the hearts do not benefit them, and He attributed the locks to the hearts because they are fitting to them. We say He meant by it specific locks, which are the locks of disbelief and obstinacy.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them, Satan has enticed them and given them false hope.﴾

This refers to the People of the Book, to whom the truth had become clear in the Torah through the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his mission, yet they turned back. Or it refers to everyone to whom the proofs appeared and who heard them but did not believe. They were a group whom love of leadership prevented from following Muhammad, peace be upon him, although they knew that he was the truth. ﴿Satan has enticed them﴾, that is, made it easy for them, ﴿and given them false hope﴾, meaning they said: "We will live for some days, then we will believe in him." It is recited as ﴿wa-amla lahum﴾ [with a fatha on the alif? no: the variant "wa-umli lahum"]. If it is said: granting respite, prolonging, and fixing the terms of life can only come from God, so how is the recitation of one who reads ﴿wa-amla lahum﴾ sound, since the one who grants respite would then be Satan? We say: the answer to this has two aspects. One: it is permissible that the intended meaning is "and God granted them respite," so one stops at ﴿has enticed them﴾.

The second: the one who enticed is also not Satan, but it is attributed to him because God decreed that it occur through his hand and tongue. So that Satan grants them respite and says to them, "In your lifetimes there is room, so enjoy your leadership, then at the end of the matter you will believe." It is also recited "wa-umli lahum," with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the hamza, in the passive form.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down: "We will obey you in part of the matter." And God knows their secret.﴾

Some exegetes said: "That" refers to the granting of respite, meaning that granting of respite is because they ﴿said to those who hated﴾. This is the choice of al-Wahidi. Others said: "That" refers to the enticing. It may be said: "That apostasy" is because they said, ﴿We will obey you﴾. This is because we explain that His saying, ﴿We will obey you in part of the matter﴾ is that they said: "We agree with you that Muhammad is not a messenger, rather he is a liar. But we will not agree with you in denying the message, the Resurrection, or associating others with God through idols. Whoever does not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) is an unbeliever, even if he believes in another." No, rather whoever does not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) does not believe in God, nor in His messengers, nor in the Resurrection. Because God, as He informed about the Resurrection, which is possible, also informed about the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, which is also possible. So whoever does not affirm God in one matter does not thereby negate falsehood from God's speech about others. Thus he is not a believer, certain of the Resurrection or of the message of any of the prophets, because the path to knowing them is one.

By ﴿those who hated what God had sent down﴾ is meant the polytheists and the hypocrites. It was also said that the intended are the Jews, since the people of Mecca said to them, "We will agree with you in expelling Muhammad, killing him, and fighting his companions." The first view is more correct, because His saying, ﴿hated what God had sent down﴾, if it were attributed to the People of the Book, would be restricted to some of what God had sent down. But if we say it is attributed to the polytheists, it is general, because they hated what God had sent down, denied all the messengers, and rejected the message entirely. His saying, ﴿We will obey you in part of the matter﴾, means in what concerns Muhammad: we will not believe in him, and we will deny him as you deny him, and fight alongside you. But as for associating others with God, taking rivals to Him from idols, and denying the Resurrection and prophethood, no.

His saying, ﴿And God knows their secret﴾: most of them said its meaning is that they said that secretly, and God exposed it and made it manifest to His Prophet, peace be upon him. The more apparent view is that it means: ﴿And God knows their secret﴾, which is what is in their hearts of knowledge of the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him, for they were arrogant and obstinate, and they knew the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as they know their own sons. It is recited "israrahum" with a kasra on the hamza, as a verbal noun (masdar). The meaning we have mentioned is clear on this recitation: they were concealing the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. On our view that those who turned back are the hypocrites, they used to say to the fighting unbelievers, ﴿We will obey you in part of the matter﴾, while concealing that if they prevailed they would turn back. As God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If there comes a victory from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed, we were with you"﴾ and He said, exalted is He: ﴿But when fear departs, they will lash you with sharp tongues﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19].

We shall mention its tafsir (exegesis) in several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah).

**The first issue:** When God, exalted is He, said, ﴿So He deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾, how could they reflect upon the Qur'an? Then He said, ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ This is like the saying of someone to a blind man, "See!" and to a deaf man, "Listen!" We say: the answer to this has three aspects, arranged so that some are better than others.

The first: imposing what cannot be borne is permissible. God commanded the one whom He knew would not believe to believe. Likewise, it is permissible that He blinds them and reproaches them for abandoning reflection.

The second: the meaning of His saying, ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ is "people."

The third: we say that this verse came to confirm the meaning of the preceding verse. He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Those are the ones whom God has cursed﴾, meaning He distanced them from Him, or from truthfulness, or from goodness, or from other good matters. ﴿So He deafened them﴾, so they do not hear the reality of speech, ﴿and blinded them﴾, so they do not follow the path of Islam. Thus they are between two states. Either they do not reflect upon the Qur'an and so they are distanced from it, because God has cursed them and distanced them from good and truthfulness, and the Qur'an is of the highest category of these, indeed the most noble kind. One is that it indicates that they are described by an attribute, because an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective is more fitting than a definite one. So it is as if He said: "upon hearts that are hard or dark."

So here He said: ﴿We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them﴾, meaning: We would make them known to you with a making-known by which you would recognize them, indicating the strength of the making-known. The first: "in the meaning of speech." In this case it is possible that what is meant by "speech" is their speech, that is, you will know them by the meaning of their words, where they say what implies hypocrisy, such as their saying when victory comes, "Indeed we were with you," and their saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], and their saying: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], and other things. The second: in the deviation of speech from what is correct, since they said what they did not believe, so they bent their speech, as when they said: ﴿We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of God. And God knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], and they said: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, and they are not exposed﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], and: ﴿And they had already made a covenant with God before, that they would not turn their backs﴾ [al-Ahzab: 15], and so on.

The third: "in the tone of speech" means in the hidden aspect of speech that the Prophet (ﷺ) understands and no one else understands. This too may bear two meanings. In it there is a subtle point: God mentioned two things, striking the faces and striking the backs, and after them mentioned two other things, following what angered God and disliking His pleasure. This is because God's mercy precedes, so He has a constant mercy, and it is the source of pleasure (ridwan), whereas God's wrath comes later, being upon a sin. So He said "His pleasure" (ridwanahu), because it is a constant attribute of God that precedes. "The pleasure of God" is a matter that proceeds from Him as an act, whereas the wrath of God is a matter that is a consequence of His act. Let us give an example: a generous man in whom generosity is firmly rooted, whose generosity moves him to good deeds. If an ill-natured person often does evil, his anger is not for a matter that returns to himself; rather his anger toward him is to reform a condition and to deter the like of him from acts like his. So it is said: he was generous, so he honored him because of the natural disposition within him; but so-and-so provoked him and anger became apparent from him. Thus anger is manifested as a result of an act, and the good act is manifested from generosity. So anger in the generous man comes after an act, and the act from him comes after generosity. From this the subtlety of His saying is known: ﴿what angered God and disliked His pleasure﴾.

Then God said: ﴿So He made their deeds fruitless﴾, since they did not seek to please God, but sought to please Satan and the idols.

This refers to the hypocrites. This is supported by the fact that a disconnected "am" hardly occurs at the beginning of a speech, so one does not say initially, "Rather Zayd came," nor "Or 'Amr came." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 47, verses 32–33:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and turn others away from the way of Allah and oppose the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them will not harm Allah at all, and He will render their deeds void.﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

The first: they are the People of the Book, the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir.

The second: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. The first view is supported by His saying: ﴿after guidance has become clear to them﴾. It has been said: the People of the Book, for the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) had become clear to them. His saying: ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾ is a threat, meaning: they think that this opposition to the Messenger, which they carry out against him, harms him, but it is not so; rather the opposition is with Allah, for Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and he is only responsible for conveying (the message). If they harm (him), they harm the (other) Messengers, but Allah is exalted above being harmed by the disbelief of a disbeliever or the wickedness of a wicked person. His saying: ﴿and He will render their deeds void﴾ — its meaning is already known. If it is said: it has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah that Allah rendered their deeds void, so how can they be rendered void in the future? We answer: the answer to this is from two angles. The first: what is meant by His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿those who disbelieve and turn others away from the way of Allah﴾, is the polytheists, who from the beginning were in falsehood, and their deeds were not according to any law. What is meant by ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ here is the People of the Book, who had deeds before the Messenger, and Allah rendered those void because of their denial of the Messenger, and their belief in the Resurrection, the Messengers and the Oneness (of God) does not benefit them. The polytheist disbeliever's deed was voided since it was not according to any law at all, nor did he acknowledge the Resurrection.

The second: that what is meant by the deeds here is their schemes in fighting, and that is with certainty on their part, but Allah will nullify it when victory belongs to the believers. And what is meant by the deeds at the beginning of the surah is what they thought to be good.

﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and do not render your deeds void.﴾

The conjunction here is of the type of attaching the consequence to the cause, as one says: "Sit and rest," "Stand and walk," because obeying Allah is entailed by obeying the Messenger. This is an indication of acting after knowledge has been attained, as if He, the Exalted, said: O you who believe, you have known the truth, so do good. His saying: ﴿and do not render your deeds void﴾ admits of several meanings:

One of them: remain upon what you are upon and do not associate (partners with Allah), lest your deeds be voided. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you associate (partners with Allah), your deeds will surely be voided﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. The second meaning: ﴿and do not render your deeds void﴾ by abandoning obedience to the Messenger, just as the People of the Book voided their deeds by denying the Messenger and disobeying him. This is supported by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], up to His saying: ﴿lest your deeds be voided while you do not perceive﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2].

The third: ﴿Do not render your charities void by reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], just as the Exalted said: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17]. This is because whoever claims a favour upon the Messenger by obedience is as if he says: "I did this for the sake of your heart, and had it not been for your approval I would not have done it," and this is contrary to sincerity, while Allah accepts only deeds that are sincere.

When He explained that the deed of the disbeliever, which has the appearance of good deeds, is nullified, and that his sin, which is the worst of evil deeds, is not forgiven, He explained that there is no sanctity (ḥurmah) for them in this world or in the Hereafter. Allah, exalted is He, has commanded obedience to the Messenger by His saying: ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾, and He commanded fighting by His saying: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, meaning: do not be feeble after the cause has come into being, in earnestness regarding the matter and striving in jihad. So He said: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾. In the verses there is an arrangement of the utmost beauty. This is because His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ necessitates striving in fighting, since the command of Allah and the command of the Messenger came with jihad, and they were ordered to obey; this necessitates that the responsible person not become weak, not be lax, not be feeble, and not be negligent. Then, after the necessitated thing, a preventing obstacle may be realized, and the caused thing may not be realized. The obstacle to fighting is either otherworldly or worldly. So He mentioned the otherworldly one, which is that the disbeliever has no sanctity in this world and the Hereafter, because he has no deed in this world and no forgiveness in the Hereafter. So when the cause exists and no obstacle is present, the caused thing should be realized. He did not place the worldly obstacle before His saying: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, as an indication that worldly matters should not be an obstacle to carrying out the command. So: do not weaken, for indeed victory is yours; or, resolve firmly, on the assumption of resolving toward defeat.

Then, after that, He, exalted is He, said: the worldly obstacle, although it should not be an obstacle, is also not present, since: (you are the superior ones). The "al-a'lawna" and "al-mustafawna" in the plural in the nominative case have a known root. It is known how the matter came to this form in inflection. This is because its original form in the regular plural is a'liyūna and mustafiyūna. The yā' was made quiescent because it is a weak letter (ḥarf 'illah), so the letter before it was vocalized, while the wāw was already quiescent, so two quiescent letters met, and there was no alternative to deleting one of them or vocalizing it. Vocalizing it would have led to the forbidden thing that was avoided, so deletion became obligatory. The wāw was there for a meaning that is conveyed only by it, which is the plural, so the yā' was dropped and a'lawna remained. By this same evidence, in the genitive it became a'linā and mustafaynā. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is with you﴾ is guidance and direction that prevents the responsible person from self-admiration. This is because when He said: ﴿And you are the superior ones﴾, that could be a cause of pride, so He said: ﴿And Allah is with you﴾, meaning: this is not from yourselves, but from Allah. Or we say: when He said: ﴿And you are the superior ones﴾, the believers saw the weakness of themselves and their small number alongside the great number and strength of the disbelievers, and some of them had the thought in their minds of how victory could be theirs. So He said: indeed Allah is with you; there should remain no doubt or misgiving that victory is yours. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I and My messengers will prevail﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21], and His saying: ﴿And indeed Our host, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173]. And His saying: ﴿and He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 35] is another promise. This is because when Allah said: indeed Allah is with you, it implied that the help comes from Allah and not from you. So the one speaking might say: I have done no deed that has any consideration, so I do not deserve honour. Then He says: He helps you, and along with that He does not diminish your deeds in any way, and He makes it as if the help were made through you and from you, so you are as if independent in that, and He gives you the reward of the one who acts on his own. The tirrah means loss, and from it comes "al-mutir", as if he had lost what would make up for him. And at the time of fighting one says: if one of the disbelievers is killed, they have been deprived (wutiru) in their family and their deeds, since their number has decreased and their deeds have been lost. The believer, if he is killed, has only diminished in number and his deeds are not diminished; and how could he be diminished in number either, since he is alive, provided for, rejoicing in what he has been led to.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and then die while they are disbelievers – never will Allah forgive them.﴾

He explains that Allah does not forgive shirk, while He forgives whatever is less than that to whomever He wills, so that no one supposes that their deeds, even if they have been nullified, are still there; rather, the grace of Allah remains, and He forgives them by His grace, even though He does not forgive them on account of their deeds.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace while you are the superior ones, and Allah is with you and will not deprive you of your deeds.﴾

When He explained that the deed of the disbeliever, which has the appearance of good deeds, is nullified, and that his sin, which is the worst of evil deeds, is not forgiven, He explained that there is no sanctity (ḥurmah) for them in this world or in the Hereafter. Allah, exalted is He, has commanded obedience to the Messenger by His saying: ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾, and He commanded fighting by His saying: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, meaning: do not be feeble after the cause has come into being, in earnestness regarding the matter and striving in jihad. So He said: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾. In the verses there is an arrangement of the utmost beauty. This is because His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ necessitates striving in fighting, since the command of Allah and the command of the Messenger came with jihad, and they were ordered to obey; this necessitates that the responsible person not become weak, not be lax, not be feeble, and not be negligent. Then, after the necessitated thing, a preventing obstacle may be realized, and the caused thing may not be realized. The obstacle to fighting is either otherworldly or worldly. So He mentioned the otherworldly one, which is that the disbeliever has no sanctity in this world and the Hereafter, because he has no deed in this world and no forgiveness in the Hereafter. So when the cause exists and no obstacle is present, the caused thing should be realized. He did not place the worldly obstacle before His saying: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, as an indication that worldly matters should not be an obstacle to carrying out the command. So: do not weaken, for indeed victory is yours; or, resolve firmly, on the assumption of resolving toward defeat.

Then, after that, He, exalted is He, said: the worldly obstacle, although it should not be an obstacle, is also not present, since: (you are the superior ones). The "al-a'lawna" and "al-mustafawna" in the plural in the nominative case have a known root. It is known how the matter came to this form in inflection. This is because its original form in the regular plural is a'liyūna and mustafiyūna. The yā' was made quiescent because it is a weak letter (ḥarf 'illah), so the letter before it was vocalized, while the wāw was already quiescent, so two quiescent letters met, and there was no alternative to deleting one of them or vocalizing it. Vocalizing it would have led to the forbidden thing that was avoided, so deletion became obligatory. The wāw was there for a meaning that is conveyed only by it, which is the plural, so the yā' was dropped and a'lawna remained. By this same evidence, in the genitive it became a'linā and mustafaynā. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is with you﴾ is guidance and direction that prevents the responsible person from self-admiration. This is because when He said: ﴿And you are the superior ones﴾, that could be a cause of pride, so He said: ﴿And Allah is with you﴾, meaning: this is not from yourselves, but from Allah. Or we say: when He said: ﴿And you are the superior ones﴾, the believers saw the weakness of themselves and their small number alongside the great number and strength of the disbelievers, and some of them had the thought in their minds of how victory could be theirs. So He said: indeed Allah is with you; there should remain no doubt or misgiving that victory is yours. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I and My messengers will prevail﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21], and His saying: ﴿And indeed Our host, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173]. And His saying: ﴿and He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 35] is another promise. This is because when Allah said: indeed Allah is with you, it implied that the help comes from Allah and not from you. So the one speaking might say: I have done no deed that has any consideration, so I do not deserve honour. Then He says: He helps you, and along with that He does not diminish your deeds in any way, and He makes it as if the help were made through you and from you, so you are as if independent in that, and He gives you the reward of the one who acts on his own. The tirrah means loss, and from it comes "al-mutir", as if he had lost what would make up for him. And at the time of fighting one says: if one of the disbelievers is killed, they have been deprived (wutiru) in their family and their deeds, since their number has decreased and their deeds have been lost. The believer, if he is killed, has only diminished in number and his deeds are not diminished; and how could he be diminished in number either, since he is alive, provided for, rejoicing in what he has been led to.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿The life of this world is but play and amusement. But if you believe and are mindful of God, He will give you your rewards, and He will not ask of you your wealth.﴾

This is an addition to the consolation, meaning: how can the world prevent you from seeking the Hereafter through jihad, when it cannot escape you, since you are victorious and dominant? And if it does escape you, your deed is not nullified. So how much more so, when what escapes you is not lost? If something is lost and not compensated, you should not turn your attention to it, because it is play and amusement. We have mentioned concerning play (la'ib) and amusement (lahw) many times that play is that with which one occupies oneself, while it has no present necessity and no benefit in the outcome. Then, if a person engages in it and it does not distract him from other things, nor divert him from his important affairs, it is play. But if it occupies him and bewilders him from his important matters, it is amusement. For this reason, the instruments of amusement are called malahi, because they are a distraction from other things. What is less than this is called play, such as playing chess (shatranj) and keeping pigeons. We have mentioned this more than once.

His saying ﴿and if you believe and are mindful of God, He will give you your rewards﴾ is a repetition of the promise. The addition (idafa) is for definiteness, meaning: the reward which He promised you in His saying ﴿a noble reward﴾ [al-Hadid: 11], ﴿a great reward﴾ [al-Mulk: 12], ﴿a great reward﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3].

His saying ﴿and He will not ask of you your wealth﴾ admits of several interpretations:

First: jihad necessarily requires expenditure. If someone says, "I will not spend my wealth," it is said to him: God does not ask of you your wealth for the specified purposes, such as zakat (obligatory almsgiving), ghanima (war booty), and the funds for public interests in what you need of wealth, which you do not account for by bringing it out.

Second: wealth belongs to God, and it is in your hands as a loan (ariya). He has requested it from you, or permitted you to spend it in the cause of jihad. So there is no sense in your stinginess with His property. An indication of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the cause of God, when to God belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Hadid: 10], meaning: all belongs to God.

Third: He does not ask of you all your wealth, but asks of you a small part of it, which is a quarter of a tenth (rub' al-'ushr). This is very little, because the tenth ('ushr) is the smallest portion, since there is no portion smaller than it, and it is not a singular noun. As for a portion of eleven, or of twelve, or up to a hundred parts, since they were not regarded, no singular name was assigned to them.

Then God, exalted is He, did not make this obligatory on the capital itself, but made it obligatory on the profit, which is from the bounty of God and His gift. Although the capital is also so, this meaning is more evident in profit. Since wealth includes what is spent for trade and what is not spent, and what is spent for trade is one of its two divisions, and it is possible that the trade in it is profitable, and possible that it is not profitable, the one division became two. So, in estimation, the profit was in a quarter of it. He therefore made obligatory a quarter of a tenth of that in which there is profit, which is a tenth. So it is a quarter of a tenth, and this is what is obligatory. Thus it is known that God does not ask of you your wealth, nor even the greater part of it.
* * *
Then He, exalted, said: ﴿If He were to ask it of you and press you, you would be stingy, and He would bring forth your spite.﴾

The fa' in His saying ﴿and He presses you﴾ indicates that pressing follows asking, as an explanation of the stinginess of souls. This is because conjunction with waw may be for two things that are alike, whereas conjunction with fa' is only for two things that follow one another or are connected, one to the other. So it is as if He, exalted, explained that pressing occurs immediately after asking, because a person, merely upon being asked, does not give anything. His saying ﴿you would be stingy and He would bring forth your spite﴾ means: He did not ask it, and even if He asked it and insisted upon you in the request, how would you be? You are stingy with the small, so you would not be generous with the large.

His saying ﴿and He would bring forth your spite﴾ means: because of it. The one asking, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, requests from you, and you, out of love for wealth and stinginess of souls, refuse. This leads to fighting, and grudges become apparent because of it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 47, verse 38:

Then Allah the Exalted said, as an elucidation of what He had said: ﴿Here you are, those who are called to spend in the way of Allah, yet among you are those who are stingy. And whoever is stingy is only stingy towards himself. And Allah is the Rich, and you are the poor.﴾

[That is to say:] I have asked of you only what is small and you were stingy; so how would it be if I asked of you everything? His words "Here you are, these" (hā'antum hā'ulā'i) may bear two meanings:

The first: that "these" (hā'ulā') is a relative pronoun, as if He said: "You are those who are called to spend in the way of Allah."

The second: that "these" (hā'ulā') alone is the predicate of "you" (antum), as one says "You are this" to affirm fame and prominence, meaning: your effect has become so manifest that there is no need to inform about you with something different. Then "you are called" (tud'awna) begins a new clause.

His words "you are called" (tud'awna) mean: called to spend, either in the way of Allah the Exalted through jihad, or in directing it to those deserving of it among your brethren. In general, in both respects there is the humiliation of the enemies and the support of the allies. ﴿Yet among you are those who are stingy.﴾ Then He explained that this stinginess is a harm that returns to the one who is stingy. So do not suppose that they withhold it from others while spending it on themselves; rather, they do not spend it even on themselves. For whoever is stingy with the physician's fee and the price of medicine while he is sick is only stingy towards himself. Then He confirmed this with His words: ﴿And Allah is the Rich﴾, not in need of your wealth, and completed it with His words: ﴿and you are the poor﴾, lest you say: "We too are rich, independent of fighting and of meeting the needs of the poor." For they have no independence from that, in this world and in the Hereafter. As for this world, it is because, were it not for fighting, they would be killed; for the disbeliever, if he does not raid, will be raided, and the needy, if he does not meet his need, will be cut off from it, especially since the Lawgiver has permitted this to the one in dire necessity. As for the Hereafter, it is evident: how could one not be poor when he is held in account and will be questioned? ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be the likes of you.﴾ The arrangement of the statement is explained in two respects:

The first: that He mentioned it as an elucidation of His self-sufficiency, as He said: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrahim: 19]. It has been mentioned that this is an affirmation after granting the premise, as if the Exalted says: Allah is independent of the entire world, so He has no need of you. If someone goes on to claim that His dominion over the world and His majesty are manifested through it, and His greatness through His servants, we say: Suppose this claim were true; yet you are not specifically determined for it. Rather, Allah is able to create a creation other than you who take pride in worshipping Him, and a world other than this which bears witness to His greatness and His grandeur.

The second: that when the Exalted had clarified the matters, established proofs for them, and made them clear through examples, He said: if you obey, you will have your rewards and more; and if you turn away, nothing remains for you but destruction. For no prophet has warned his people and they persisted in denying him without the word of destruction being decreed against them, and Allah cleansing the earth of them and bringing other people who are pure.

His words "then they will not be the likes of you" (thumma lā yakūnū amthālakum) contain a grammatical issue from which precious benefits become clear. The grammarians have said: it is permissible for what is conjoined to the answer of the conditional with wa, fa, or thumma to be both jazm (jussive) and raf' (nominative). Allah the Exalted said here: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be the likes of you﴾ with jazm (lā yakūnū, without nūn), and He said in another place: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111] with raf' by affirming the nūn (yunṣarūna), and this is with permissibility. In it there is a refinement: here "lā yakūnū" is not connected to "tawallī" (turning away), for if they do not turn away they will be among those whom Allah brings to obedience, and if they turn away they will not be like them, because they are disobedient, [which is] the condition of those whom He brings obedient. As for there, whether they fight or do not fight, they will not be helped; so there was no sense of conditionality there, and it was therefore put in the raf' by the inceptive, whereas here it is jazm for conditionality.

His words "then they will not be the likes of you" (thumma lā yakūnū amthālakum) allow two meanings: The first: that the intended meaning is "then they will not be your likes" in attribute and not in kind, and this is fitting. The second meaning, and in it are several views:

The first: a people of non-Arabs (ʿajam).

The second: a people of Persia. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about those who would be substituted for them if they turned away, while Salman was beside him, and he said: "This one and his people." Then he said: "If faith were suspended from the Pleiades, men from Persia would attain it."

The third: a people of the Ansar, and Allah knows best.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon the best of His creation, Muhammad the Prophet, and upon his family, companions, and kin, all of them, and peace be upon them abundantly. Amen.
